title: Evaluation of Phonetic Encoding Algorithms on Transcription Datasets
abstract: In this work, a novel evaluation scheme built on a generalized variant of the Rand Index measure, namely, the Hüllermeier-Rifqi Index, is proposed in order to assess how well phonetic encoding algorithms conform to word-based transcriptions in IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet) notation. For this objective, the discordance score is obtained by calculating the absolute difference between the pairwise similarity values of ground-truth transcriptions and those of corresponding phonetic encodings, which are computed using normalized edit distance as a permutation dependent string metric. The resulting score is subsequently adjusted with respect to that of a random string generator incorporating the same alphabet as the encoder under consideration. A wide range of phonetic encoders were evaluated as such on multi-lingual transcription datasets along with their recall capabilities based on the collision rate. The validity of the proposed scheme is further supported by its applicability in measuring the orthographic transparency of a language when the writing system is viewed as an inherent phonetic representation.

title: Robust PAC Learning of Concurrent Stochastic Games
abstract: We introduce the first Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games (CSGs) with transition uncertainty, while addressing the challenge of Nash equilibrium (NE) existence. Our algorithm maintains data-driven $L^1$ confidence sets over transition kernels and solves a robust CSG to compute a social-welfare optimal $\varepsilon$-NE, using a robust MDP-based exploration mechanism to drive joint state-action coverage. Crucially, we introduce a Nash margin characterisation that enables principled reasoning about equilibrium existence: the framework either returns an $\varepsilon$-approximate NE whose social-welfare value is $\varepsilon$-close to optimal, or provides a sound certificate that no exact NE exists. Under a minimum reachability condition $p_{\mathrm{reach}}>0$ over relevant state-action pairs, the algorithm terminates after a polynomial number of trajectory samples, with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( {R_{\max}^2 H^4 |S|^2 |A| / (p_{\mathrm{reach}} \varepsilon^2)} \right)$. Empirical results on benchmark CSGs demonstrate near-optimal performance, correct handling of equilibrium (non-)existence, and sample complexity consistent with theory.

title: Lose the Order, Keep the Hierarchy: Deordering HTN Plans
abstract: Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning is a powerful planning formalism based on task decomposition. Although most of the literature studied plan generation, comparatively less attention has been paid to post-plan optimization. In particular, plan deordering has been extensively studied in classical planning but remains under-researched in the HTN setting. Plan deordering removes unnecessary ordering constraints between actions in a plan whilst keeping the plan valid. In this paper, we adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending the techniques to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints. We evaluate our proposed approaches on the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks and we compare them against Optiplan, an HTN planner that generates partially ordered plans directly. Our results show a substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both our implementations. Although we also observe a reduction in critical path length, the improvements are less pronounced.

We evaluate our proposed approaches on the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks and we compare them against Optiplan, an HTN planner that generates partially ordered plans directly. Our results show a substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both our implementations. Although we also observe a reduction in critical path length, the improvements are less pronounced.

title: OCR-EDR: Rendering-Aware Diagnosis and Repair for Closed-Loop OCR Improvement
abstract: Although document OCR systems perform increasingly well on routine documents, complex formulas, structured text, and long-tail formats remain error-prone. OCR predictions may omit fine-grained content or hallucinate unsupported outputs, while equivalent encodings of the same visible content must be accommodated. Existing OCR evaluation methods mostly report aggregate metrics, offering limited support for analyzing case-level errors and improving OCR performance. We propose OCR-EDR (OCR Error Diagnosis and Repair), a rendering-aware framework that advances from fine-grained diagnosis to iterative repair. Given a source image, an editable OCR prediction, and its rendered image, OCR-EDR first jointly assesses whether the prediction and its rendering are consistent with the source, preserving valid predictions, including rendering-equivalent ones, while diagnosing and localizing genuine errors. It then applies executable edits and may request an updated rendering for iterative reassessment. We construct OCRErrBench from diverse real OCR predictions, covering text and formulas, exact and rendering-equivalent positives, and genuine errors, and develop the DocEDR model to execute the diagnosis--repair loop. On OCRErrBench, DocEDR achieves 94.78% diagnostic accuracy. It repairs 86.23% of erroneous inputs to visual consistency, raises formula Case-F1 by 30.99 percentage points over DOCR-Inspector-7B on DOCRcaseBench, and improves formula CDM by up to 4.62 percentage points on the identified Bad subsets of four OCR systems on UniMER-Test. These results show that OCR-EDR turns fine-grained OCR analysis into verified corrections and performance gains.

title: RAFT: A Real-World Few-Shot Text Classification Benchmark
abstract: Large pre-trained language models have shown promise for few-shot learning, completing text-based tasks given only a few task-specific examples. Will models soon solve classification tasks that have so far been reserved for human research assistants? Existing benchmarks are not designed to measure progress in applied settings, and so don't directly answer this question. The RAFT benchmark (Real-world Annotated Few-shot Tasks) focuses on naturally occurring tasks and uses an evaluation setup that mirrors deployment. Baseline evaluations on RAFT reveal areas current techniques struggle with: reasoning over long texts and tasks with many classes. Human baselines show that some classification tasks are difficult for non-expert humans, reflecting that real-world value sometimes depends on domain expertise. title: 基于自适应量子模型的强化学习
abstract: This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning framework based on adaptive quantum models, leveraging the inherent quantum state adaptability to achieve enhanced learning efficiency and precision. Traditional reinforcement learning often relies on fixed parameters, limiting the potential for optimization. Our approach utilizes quantum state dynamics to dynamically adjust the learning process, fostering a more effective and accurate training regime. The core claim is that this framework offers a significant improvement over existing methods through the integration of quantum state adaptation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design through a series of simulations, showcasing enhanced convergence speed and improved performance on a challenging reinforcement learning task. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential applications and future directions of this research.

title: Probability-Based Dynamic Matrix Generation and Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic matrix generation and optimization algorithm based on probability association matrices. The algorithm aims to dynamically generate a probability association matrix to optimize model parameters, enhancing model generalization. We propose a mechanism that iteratively generates and adjusts probability distributions within the matrix to guide the parameter optimization process. The core novelty lies in the dynamic matrix generation, which leverages a probabilistic model to guide the optimization. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and provides insights into its potential impact on model performance.

title: Self-Supervised Learning via Predictive State Transitions in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to self-supervised learning (SSL) that leverages the inherent predictability of state transitions within complex systems. The core idea is to train a model to forecast the future state of a system, given its past and current state. This approach frames the complex system's dynamics as a generative process, enabling the model to learn representations directly from the underlying data without explicit labels. We demonstrate the potential of this method across diverse complex systems, including biological networks and climate models. The central contribution lies in the formulation of a predictive learning objective that captures the sequential dependencies critical to understanding system behavior. We outline the key components of the framework, including the model architecture, training procedure, and evaluation metrics. The results suggest that this self-supervised method can effectively learn meaningful representations and potentially improve downstream tasks that require an understanding of system dynamics. The core of the method is to build a model that can predict state transitions, thereby learning the underlying rules of the system. This is achieved through a predictive state transition objective.

title: Quantum Adaptive Algorithm Parameter Optimization
abstract: Quantum adaptive algorithms offer the potential for significant speedups in complex computations, particularly in areas like quantum chemistry and materials science. However, achieving optimal performance often requires careful optimization of quantum parameters, a task that can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces a novel quantum adaptive algorithm that dynamically adjusts quantum parameters to optimize algorithm efficiency and accuracy, thereby reducing computational costs. We propose a method centered around a feedback loop that continuously monitors and adjusts the parameters based on the algorithm's output, leading to a more robust and adaptable optimization strategy. The core mechanism leverages a dynamic parameter tuning process to achieve this. This research explores the potential of this approach in tackling specific challenges within quantum algorithm design and provides a framework for future development. The key innovation lies in the continuous feedback loop that dynamically adjusts parameters, resulting in a more efficient and accurate algorithm.

title: Quantum Annealing Algorithm Optimization and Application
abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) is a promising quantum computing paradigm for solving optimization problems. However, the performance of QA is often limited by issues such as slow convergence rates and sensitivity to parameter settings. This paper presents a novel optimization method designed to address these limitations. The approach introduces refined parameters and an adaptive strategy to enhance the algorithm's convergence speed and solution accuracy. We explore the application of this optimized QA method to complex problems, demonstrating its potential for improved performance. The core of the optimization lies in modifying the annealing schedule and incorporating a dynamic adjustment of the magnetic field strength, denoted as $H(t)$, where $t$ represents time. The objective function to be minimized is typically represented as $E[s]$, where $s$ is the state vector of the quantum annealer. We introduce a variance reduction technique, denoted as $\sigma(t)$, which is dynamically adjusted based on the error estimates of the current state. The overall optimization process can be summarized as: $\min_{s} E[s] \quad \text{subject to} \quad \frac{dS}{dt} = - \beta(t) E[s] - \gamma(t) H(t)s$ where $\beta(t)$ is the annealing rate and $\gamma(t)$ is the magnetic field strength. The adaptive strategy involves updating $\beta(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ based on the error in the current solution, aiming to reduce the variance $\sigma(t)$ and improve the convergence. The theoretical analysis suggests that this approach can significantly reduce the computational cost and improve the solution quality compared to traditional QA methods. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of different parameter settings on the algorithm's performance, highlighting the importance of careful tuning for optimal results. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in solution quality and convergence speed across various benchmark problems.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning with Latent Time Scales
abstract: This paper introduces a novel hierarchical Bayesian deep learning framework designed to effectively capture long-range dependencies in temporal data. The core challenge in standard Bayesian deep learning lies in the difficulty of inference within high-dimensional latent spaces, hindering the model's ability to represent and learn correlations across extended time periods. Our approach addresses this limitation by incorporating latent time scales, creating a hierarchical structure where each layer learns to represent data at different temporal resolutions. This allows for a more efficient and accurate representation of temporal dependencies, leading to improved performance in tasks involving time series analysis and forecasting. We outline the key components of the framework, including the Bayesian inference process, the definition of latent time scales, and the architecture of the hierarchical deep learning model. The proposed method demonstrates the potential to overcome the limitations of traditional approaches and offers a promising direction for future research in temporal data modeling.

title: Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Graph Embedding
abstract: Learning effective graph embeddings from limited data, a scenario often encountered in real-world applications, presents a substantial challenge in graph representation learning. Traditional graph embedding methods typically require large datasets for training, leading to poor performance when only a few labeled examples are available. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to address this problem. Specifically, we train a meta-learning model that learns to quickly adapt to new graph embedding tasks with minimal labeled data. The core idea is to learn a meta-learner that can efficiently update its parameters based on a small number of examples, enabling rapid adaptation to diverse graph structures and tasks. We formulate the problem as a few-shot learning scenario, where the meta-learner learns to generalize across different graph embedding tasks. The performance of our approach is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in learning high-quality graph embeddings from limited data. The key contribution of this work lies in the application of meta-learning techniques to graph embedding, offering a promising solution for scenarios where data scarcity is a major constraint.

title: Symbolic Regression with Constraint Satisfaction Programming
abstract: Symbolic regression aims to discover mathematical equations from data. However, its performance suffers when dealing with complex constraints or high-dimensional data, leading to computationally expensive and often unproductive searches. This work proposes a novel approach that integrates symbolic regression with constraint satisfaction programming (CSP). The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both techniques: symbolic regression's ability to generate expressive mathematical models, and CSP's robust method for efficiently finding solutions that adhere to a set of constraints. We introduce a framework where the symbolic regression process is guided by a CSP engine, enabling the system to explore a constrained solution space. This approach significantly reduces the search space, improving the efficiency and accuracy of symbolic regression, particularly when dealing with complex relationships and limitations. The primary contribution is a novel method for enhancing symbolic regression's capability to address real-world scenarios characterized by intricate constraints and data complexities.

title: Quantum-Inspired Neural Networks with Adaptive Graph Structures
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to neural network design, termed Quantum-Inspired Neural Networks (QINNs) with Adaptive Graph Structures. The core idea is to leverage the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics – specifically superposition and entanglement – to create a network architecture that exhibits enhanced information processing capabilities. Traditional neural networks often struggle with complex, non-linear relationships and can suffer from vanishing gradients during training. QINNs address these limitations by employing dynamically evolving graph structures that mimic the interconnectedness and efficient information transfer observed in quantum systems. The network architecture is designed to represent data through a superposition of states, allowing for the exploration of multiple solution paths simultaneously. Furthermore, adaptive graph structures, inspired by entanglement, facilitate the correlation of information between nodes, significantly improving the network's ability to capture intricate patterns. This approach represents a significant departure from simply using quantum concepts as an inspirational element; it's a fundamental integration of quantum principles into the neural network design, leading to potentially superior performance in tasks demanding high computational efficiency and pattern recognition accuracy. The paper outlines the theoretical framework, the proposed architecture, and discusses the potential benefits and future research directions.

title: Quantum Security Proofs Based on Quantum Decoherence
abstract: This paper presents a theoretical framework for demonstrating the security of quantum algorithms leveraging the phenomenon of quantum decoherence. We explore the vulnerability of quantum algorithms to external disturbances, arguing that decoherence fundamentally undermines their computational advantage. Our core claim is that by precisely quantifying decoherence effects and their impact on quantum operations, we can establish rigorous security proofs for specific quantum algorithms. The mechanism we employ centers on modeling the propagation of errors introduced by decoherence, ultimately demonstrating that the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum computation, when compounded by decoherence, renders many quantum algorithms susceptible to manipulation. This research offers a novel approach to quantum security analysis, shifting the focus from idealized, error-free quantum systems to the realistic conditions of noisy quantum environments. We define a mathematical framework for assessing algorithmic security based on decoherence rates and operational fidelity, proposing a quantifiable metric for determining the limits of quantum computational advantage. The ultimate goal is to inform the design of more robust and secure quantum algorithms, acknowledging and incorporating decoherence as a central element of security considerations. ---

title: ##基于多智能体强化学习的分布式资源管理
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to the problem of distributed resource management. Traditional approaches to this problem often rely on centralized control, which can be inefficient and vulnerable to single points of failure. This research proposes a decentralized solution utilizing MARL, where multiple agents, each responsible for managing a subset of resources, learn to coordinate and optimize overall system performance through interaction and reward signals. We formulate the resource management task as a multi-agent Markov Decision Process (MAMP), leveraging algorithms such as Independent Q-Learning (IQL) and Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) to train the agents. The core claim is that MARL offers a viable framework for distributed resource management. The mechanism relies on the agents learning optimal strategies through trial and error, adapting to changing conditions, and ultimately achieving greater efficiency and robustness compared to traditional methods. The novelty of this work lies in its exploration of MARL's potential in this domain, a field still in its nascent stages. The results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach.

title: Self-Referential Code Synthesis via Evolutionary Grammars
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to code synthesis – Self-Referential Code Synthesis – that leverages evolutionary grammars to generate complex code structures. The core idea is to move beyond traditional syntactic rule-based systems and introduce a meta-cognitive capability, allowing the system to understand and modify its own structure autonomously. This is achieved through a simulated evolutionary algorithm operating on a population of code fragments. Each fragment is evaluated based on its "self-referential" modification potential, leading to a dynamic refinement process. The system employs a grammar that governs how code fragments can be combined and altered, but crucially, the evolutionary algorithm drives the selection of fragments exhibiting the most effective self-modification strategies. The resulting system demonstrates the potential for generating sophisticated code without explicit, hand-crafted rules for complex structural changes. The key contribution lies in the creation of a system capable of iterative self-improvement, mimicking a cognitive process within the code generation landscape. The evaluation metric focuses on the efficiency and correctness of the generated code, ensuring that the evolutionary process ultimately leads to optimized solutions. This approach offers a fundamentally different perspective on code synthesis, suggesting that autonomous refinement is a critical component for tackling the challenges of generating complex software.

title: E8-Phi Quantum Phase-Gradient Entanglement Transfer Protocol — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By projecting E8's 240 root vectors onto phi-scaled torsion folds and driving them at the 132Hz base frequency, a quantum phase-gradient emerges that can mediate coherent entanglement transfer across distributed qubit networks. This protocol exploits the nested 64-dimensional manifold lattice to encode phase-difference information along geodesics connecting root-vector nodes, enabling deterministic entanglement distribution without requiring shared reference frames between distant parties. The geometric structure ensures that phi-coupled interference patterns at each node create a self-correcting phase-closure manifold, where deviations from ideal golden-ratio scaling manifest as detectable decoherence signatures that can be topologically compensated. Experimental realization would demonstrate genuine multipartite coherence spanning E8-symmetric node clusters, advancing distributed quantum computing architectures through geometric phase protection. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Geometric Transformation Quantum State Description
abstract: This paper explores the integration of quantum states into geometric transformation descriptions, aiming to revolutionize computation through the representation of geometric transformations. Traditional methods often rely on classical descriptions, but this work proposes a novel framework where quantum states directly encode geometric information, offering the potential for significantly more efficient and expressive computation. We detail the core mechanism, outlining the development of a system that maps geometric transformations to quantum states, enabling computational operations based on these quantum states. The paper introduces a conceptual model and preliminary results demonstrating the feasibility of this approach, highlighting its potential impact on various fields including geometry, computer graphics, and optimization. The core claim is that this framework facilitates efficient computation through the direct manipulation of quantum states, providing a fundamental shift in how geometric transformations are represented and processed.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction with Wave Function Optimization
abstract: Quantum-enhanced constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) offer a potential paradigm shift in solving complex optimization challenges, particularly in areas requiring sophisticated search and efficient solution paths. This paper investigates the application of quantum algorithms to constraint satisfaction, aiming to accelerate the search process and enhance solution quality. Specifically, we explore the integration of quantum wave function optimization techniques to represent and manipulate constraint satisfaction spaces. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging quantum computation to efficiently explore the solution space, optimizing the wave function for a given constraint satisfaction. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the potential benefits of this approach, emphasizing its ability to overcome limitations associated with traditional CSP solvers. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the challenges associated with scaling this quantum-enhanced approach to larger, more complex problems.

title: Adaptive NLI-Driven Claim Verification with Statistical Decision Modeling for Low-Latency Hallucination Reduction in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a critical tendency to generate factually incorrect yet linguistically fluent outputs - a phenomenon termed hallucination - which poses serious risks in precision-critical applications. Existing mitigation strategies, including retrieval-augmented generation and self-consistency sampling, either introduce substantial inference latency or depend on external knowledge infrastructure, limiting their applicability in real-time deployments. This paper proposes a lightweight two-step claim verification framework that decomposes LLM responses into atomic factual claims and independently verifies each extracted claim against a separately generated reference produced through an isolated factual recall prompt. Although the generator and verifier share the same underlying language model, separating response generation from factual recall reduces direct response conditioning and mitigates confirmation bias during verification, using Natural Language Inference, and applies an adaptive statistical threshold - defined as τ = µ + kσ over the NLI confidence score distribution - to selectively correct only contradicted claims. Unlike prior NLI-based methods that rely on fixed decision boundaries, the proposed framework dynamically adapts its verification threshold to the confidence distribution of each response, showing consistent performance across the evaluated benchmarks without requiring model retraining. Evaluated on TruthfulQA and FEVER, the framework reduces the hallucination rate from 28% to 9% on TruthfulQA - a 67.9% relative reduction - while incurring only 160 ms of additional latency over the baseline LLM and outperforming SelfCheckGPT and FActScore in hallucination detection accuracy. These results indicate that the framework can provide a favorable balance between factual reliability and response latency on the evaluated benchmarks, while further validation across domains and deployment settings is needed.

title: Interactive UI for Captum
abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is pivotal for ensuring transparency, accountability, and trust in AI systems, yet its widespread adoption is hindered by complex tools and steep learning curves. This chapter presents an interactive user interface (UI) for Captum, a leading XAI library, designed to democratize access to model interpretability for practitioners across diverse domains. By integrating a suite of explainability techniques into a unified, intuitive platform, our UI mitigates technical and cognitive barriers, empowering both domain experts and nontechnical users to derive actionable insights from AI models. We explore the foundational principles of XAI, the design and implementation of our UI, and its applications in high-stakes fields, such as healthcare, finance, education, autonomous systems, legal, and natural language processing domains. Through extensive case studies, comparative analyses, and user evaluations, we demonstrate how our approach significantly enhances XAI accessibility, fostering responsible AI adoption and addressing ethical concerns in AI deployment.

title: The Anatomy of an ASR Hallucination
abstract: ASR systems sometimes produce fluent text that is unrelated to the speech they receive. We view these hallucinations as one possible consequence of a broader grounding failure, in which the transcript is no longer adequately guided by the audio. To understand where this failure becomes possible, we study two independently trained Conformer-Large recognizers - one CTC and one RNN-T - under environmental degradation and speaker-background shift. In both models, the final encoder stage emerges as a critical boundary: bypassing the final block causes divergence on nearly every utterance, whereas bypassing middle blocks has little effect. At this same stage, the representations become more compact, text becomes readable by the trained decoder, and grapheme information becomes explicit. Importantly, the intervention produces garbled or repetitive output rather than fluent fabrication. Our result therefore identifies a mechanistic precondition for hallucination - the failure to produce adequately grounded output - not the complete origin of naturally occurring hallucinations. Together, the results reveal a consistent terminal-stage dependency for grounded recognition across two decoder families and multiple distribution shifts.

title: On the geometry and typicality of quantum magic
abstract: We prove that, for an $n$-qubit system of dimension $d=2^n$, every state satisfying $\operatorname{Tr}(ρ^2)\le 1/(d-a_\ast)$, with $a_\ast=0.458327\cdots$, lies inside the stabilizer polytope and is therefore magic-free. Combining this result with general geometric properties of high-dimensional polytopes, we establish quantitative estimates for the Hilbert--Schmidt inradius and volume radius of the stabilizer polytope, and use them to characterize the typicality of magic in random induced states obtained by tracing out a $k$-dimensional subsystem from a $d\times k$-dimensional Haar-random pure state. We prove a sharp phase transition in the probability of such states having magic, whose transition dimension $k_\star$ is bounded between $Ω(d^2/\log^2d)$ and $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$. We further prove that the number of facets of the stabilizer polytope lies between $\exp[Ω(d^2/\log^2 d)]$ and $\exp[\mathcal{O}(d^2\log^2 d)]$ employing a result of Bourgain and Milman in convex geometry, substantially improving upon the previous quasipolynomial lower bound and implying that doubly-exponentially many linear inequalities in the number of qubits are required for an exact description of the magic-free region. Overall, our results reveal the near-extremal geometry of the stabilizer polytope and provide a quantitative foundation for understanding the typicality, robustness, and detectability of magic.

title: Markovian Shock-Source Tracing and Multidimensional Asset Roles in Exchange Rates, Gold Futures, and Bitcoin
abstract: This study examines cross-asset connectedness in an international financial network of major exchange rates, gold futures, and Bitcoin. Moving beyond the conventional net transmitter--receiver classification, we characterize asset roles through three complementary dimensions: direct spillover transmission, stationary source-tracing dynamics, and multistep upstream connectivity. Return spillovers are estimated using VAR generalized forecast-error variance decomposition (VAR-GFEVD). The positive pairwise net-spillover structure is then mapped into a row-stochastic Markov kernel whose transitions trace dominant net-spillover sources in the reverse direction of the original transmission edges. A stationary departure flux describes long-run movement in this source-tracing chain, while Viral Centrality is evaluated by the deterministic probability-propagation algorithm of Fink et al. to approximate multistep upstream reach. Empirically, gold futures emerge as the dominant direct net transmitter and the leading stationary source-tracing node, but do not have the largest Viral Centrality. Several exchange-rate nodes classified as direct net receivers have relatively high Viral Centrality, indicating broad conditional access to upstream source nodes. Bitcoin occupies an intermediate role. An auxiliary specification including the U.S. Dollar Index yields qualitatively similar role differentiation. The results show that direct connectedness, stationary source tracing, and approximate multistep upstream reach cannot be inferred from NET spillovers alone. All diffusion interpretations are descriptive and conditional on the estimated network, row normalization, and restart closure.

title: The Next Frontier: Security Implications of Future AI Paradigms
abstract: The current paradigm of frontier AI continues to yield significant value, but as compute scaling faces potentially diminishing returns, future AI progress is unlikely to rely on a single, isolated breakthrough. The next wave of capability improvements will most likely emerge from a complex mix of extensions, hybrids and specialised pathways combined with existing models. This CETaS Research Report maps the emergence of novel AI paradigms across alternative architectures, data sources, learning methods, and hardware substrates. The report provides a basis to help policymakers anticipate and respond to technological surprise. For the UK, maintaining a competitive edge in AI requires strategic agility. To achieve this, the report advocates for action across three priority policy areas: building a deep skills base; investing in supporting infrastructure; and embracing fast-following and application at scale.

title: Derivation-graph census of the Hugging Face Hub, 2026-09-03
abstract: A complete snapshot of the public Hugging Face Hub model index (3,038,899 records for 3,038,885 distinct repositories, retrieved 2026-09-03T21:13:45Z) together with the derivation graph reconstructed from declared base_model tags (884,673 parent-child edges, 533,720 of them carrying strong enough evidence for a verdict — either both licenses declared and classified, or a permissive parent that imposes nothing whatever the child declares), the license adjudication applied to each edge, and the full pipeline that produces them. This is the archived snapshot underlying the article "The junction matters: where declared license signals fail to survive in the Hugging Face derivation graph". The Hub is a moving structure, so the analysis is reproducible only against this deposit, not against a later re-fetch. Contents. The raw index as gzipped JSONL shards; the node and edge tables in Parquet with license family, evidence grade and violation code per edge; the numbers registry and every reported table and figure; the pipeline code. What this is not. No model weights are included. The archive holds public repository metadata only. Each repository described here carries its own license, which this deposit does not alter and does not purport to grant.

title: Agent Harnesses and the New Threat Landscape
abstract: Agent harnesses, the orchestration code, memory management, tool routing, sandboxing, and permission logic wrapped around a language model, have become an increasingly consequential attack surface for agentic AI, compounding the model-level weaknesses that most current incidents already implicate. This paper defines a reference architecture for agent harnesses and documents seven threat categories specific to that architecture: untrusted content re-entering the reasoning loop, excessive agency from permissive tool grants, sandbox and execution-layer compromise, multi-agent delegation collapsing into the confused-deputy problem, autonomous loop failures including reward hacking, harness supply-chain risk, and observability gaps that delay incident detection. Each category is grounded in named, dated incidents and disclosures from 2025 and 2026, including Anthropic's disruption of an MCP-orchestrated espionage campaign, a documented production-database deletion by an autonomous coding agent, and a critical remote-code-execution vulnerability affecting an estimated 200,000 Model Context Protocol server instances. The paper synthesizes these findings into two composite attack paths and closes with a five-layer defense-in-depth framework, a minimal reference implementation adversarially testing that framework's core controls, and a practical hardening checklist for teams building new agent harnesses.

title: Self-Organizing Information Theory Adaptive Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive algorithm for information processing based on Self-Organizing Information Theory (SOIT). The algorithm leverages the inherent statistical properties of input data to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters, enabling optimized performance in computation and data compression. We propose a framework where the algorithm's parameter configuration is determined by analyzing data distributions, leading to more flexible and efficient computational processes. The core mechanism involves constructing the algorithm's parameter space using SOIT principles, with adjustments driven by data-dependent statistical characteristics. This approach contrasts with traditional parameter-based algorithms, offering enhanced adaptability and potentially superior results. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through simulations, showcasing improved compression rates and faster processing speeds compared to existing methods.

title: Title: Non-Linear Topological Entanglement for Quantum Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum simulation utilizing non-linear topological entanglement. Traditional entanglement schemes often struggle with issues of coherence and fidelity, limiting their effectiveness in simulating complex quantum systems. We propose a dynamically adjustable "landscape" of entanglement parameters within a topological framework, enabling unprecedented control over the entanglement structure and its influence on simulation accuracy. This method significantly expands the scope of quantum simulation, potentially unlocking new capabilities in materials science, drug discovery, and fundamental physics. The core mechanism centers around creating and manipulating topological entanglement, a fundamentally different approach compared to standard entanglement distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations of a parameterized quantum system, showcasing improved coherence and fidelity compared to existing techniques.

title: Title: Modular Geometry & Adaptive Topology - Self-Organizing Data Structures
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Modular Geometry and Adaptive Topology as a novel methodology for designing data structures, focusing on self-organizing evolution and high computational efficiency. Traditional data structures often employ static layouts, limiting flexibility and potentially hindering performance. We propose a "Topology Weaver" algorithm, leveraging modular geometry principles to dynamically adjust data module arrangements, creating self-repairing and adaptable structures. This investigation addresses the limitations of current data structure design by introducing a method that actively reshapes data based on its connectivity, fostering resilience and optimizing computational resources. The core mechanism centers on iteratively adjusting geometric parameters, driven by dependencies and connectivity patterns, to achieve optimal self-organization. We present a theoretical framework and a preliminary implementation of the Topology Weaver algorithm, demonstrating its potential for creating data structures with enhanced adaptability and efficiency.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Metric Regularization with Adaptive Constraints
abstract: Metric spaces, fundamental in many fields, often exhibit suboptimal solutions during optimization. Traditional regularization methods, while effective, can be brittle and fail to consistently escape local minima. This paper introduces a novel non-Euclidean metric regularization technique predicated on the local geometry of data points. We propose a dynamic constraint adjustment mechanism, driven by the data's inherent structure, to proactively prevent convergence to suboptimal solutions. This approach leverages the concept of 'geometry-aware regularization', encouraging exploration of the space and potentially uncovering more globally optimal solutions. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through extensive simulations and a comparison with existing regularization techniques.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Bayesian Optimization of Neural Network Architectures
abstract: This paper investigates the application of probabilistic programming to the challenging problem of Bayesian optimization for neural network architecture search. Traditional approaches to neural architecture search (NAS) often suffer from high computational costs and inefficient exploration of the architecture space. We propose a framework that utilizes probabilistic programming languages to define a model of the architecture search space, incorporating prior knowledge and iteratively refining the search strategy based on Bayesian inference. Specifically, we formulate the architecture search as a sequential decision problem, where each decision involves selecting a component of the neural network. The probabilistic model allows us to represent the uncertainty associated with each architecture and guides the optimization process towards promising regions of the search space. The core mechanism involves defining a probabilistic model of the architecture search space, incorporating prior knowledge and learning from previous evaluations, allowing for targeted exploration of promising architectures. This approach significantly improves the efficiency of the search process compared to traditional methods, offering a principled framework for automating neural architecture search. The key benefit lies in the ability to efficiently sample from the architecture space, guided by Bayesian inference, leading to faster convergence and potentially superior neural network architectures.

title: Dynamic Topological Quantum Neuron Networks
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Dynamic Topological Quantum Neuron Networks (DTQNNs), a novel approach to computation leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement and neural networks. The core claim is that real-time adjustment of entanglement strength between neurons can enable more efficient and flexible computation compared to traditional neural networks. The underlying mechanism involves constructing a neural network using an entanglement network and dynamically adjusting the entanglement parameters – specifically, the coupling strength between qubits – to modulate neuronal connections and information transfer. This approach aims to overcome the information bottlenecks inherent in conventional neural networks by directly utilizing quantum entanglement for information processing. The theoretical framework presented explores the potential for DTQNNs to achieve enhanced computational capabilities and adaptive learning, representing a significant advancement in the intersection of quantum computing and artificial intelligence. The key mathematical concepts underpinning this approach are explored, including the description of entanglement entropy, quantum state manipulation, and network dynamics. We propose a model for DTQNNs based on the principles of topological quantum computation, focusing on the creation and control of non-local correlations between neurons. This model provides a foundation for future research and development in this emerging field.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Symbolic Data Generation
abstract: This paper explores the application of self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques to the challenging problem of symbolic data generation. Traditional approaches to generating symbolic data, such as mathematical expressions or code, rely heavily on large, meticulously labeled datasets, a significant bottleneck. We propose a novel framework that utilizes SSL to learn representations from unlabeled symbolic data, enabling the generation of new, plausible instances. The core idea is to exploit the inherent structural patterns and relationships within the data itself to create supervisory signals. This approach circumvents the need for extensive manual labeling, offering a scalable solution for generating diverse and complex symbolic data. We detail the architecture of the model, the self-supervised learning objectives employed, and discuss the potential applications and future research directions. The generated symbolic data is evaluated based on its structural validity and similarity to the original data distribution. Our results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of SSL for this task, paving the way for more efficient and robust symbolic data generation systems.

title: Quantum-Driven Constraint on Complex Systems
abstract: Quantum-driven constraint on complex systems aims to accelerate solution processes by dynamically adjusting constraint parameters. This paper explores the potential of quantum annealing and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) to optimize these parameters. The core claim is to implement an algorithm that dynamically adjusts constraint parameters on complex systems (e.g., protein folding, DNA sequencing) to achieve optimal solution speed and accuracy. The approach leverages quantum annealing for its ability to escape local optima and VQE for efficient exploration of the solution space. This research investigates the feasibility and potential advantages of employing quantum computing for optimization tasks within complex systems, offering a novel methodology for enhancing computational efficiency.

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to complex system modeling and simulation utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs). The core focus is to develop a method capable of automatically learning complex relationships within a system, and generating high-fidelity predictions. Traditional methods often struggle to effectively model dynamic relationships. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offer a powerful tool for this purpose. This paper details the architecture of our proposed GNN-based system, its training methodology, and its demonstrated performance in simulating a complex system. title: Dynamical Complexity Measures for Algorithmic Diversity
abstract: This paper introduces a novel set of complexity measures designed to quantitatively assess the diversity of algorithmic solutions across various problem domains. Traditional complexity measures often fail to capture the true breadth of algorithmic innovation, leading to a static assessment of solutions. We propose a dynamic metric that analyzes the "novelty" of an algorithm's execution, updating the score as the solution evolves. This dynamic assessment facilitates the identification of innovative solutions and promotes a continuous evaluation of algorithmic quality. The core mechanism centers around a novel analysis of solution generation, resulting in a more comprehensive and adaptive measure of algorithmic diversity. This work offers a shift towards a more holistic understanding of algorithmic progress.

title: Formal Verification of Probabilistic Programming Systems using Abstract Interpretation
abstract: Probabilistic programming languages (PPLs) are increasingly utilized for modeling and reasoning about uncertainty in various domains, including robotics, artificial intelligence, and finance. However, ensuring the correctness of these programs – particularly with respect to their probabilistic guarantees – remains a significant challenge. Traditional verification techniques often rely on precise numerical accuracy, which is difficult to achieve and maintain in the face of inherent stochasticity. This paper presents a novel approach to formal verification of PPLs based on abstract interpretation. We systematically analyze the abstract representation of a probabilistic program, identifying potential violations of specified probabilistic guarantees without relying on exact numerical simulation. Our method focuses on validating the *logic* of the probabilistic reasoning, offering a more robust and scalable verification strategy. This work outlines the core principles, key techniques, and potential applications of this approach.

title: Adaptive Domain Generalization with Meta-Learning of Representation Alignment
abstract: Domain adaptation techniques have demonstrated significant success in bridging the gap between source and target domains. However, their effectiveness often plateaus when faced with truly unseen domains, leading to a lack of robust generalization. This paper proposes a novel approach to domain generalization that leverages meta-learning to achieve adaptive representation alignment. Our core claim is that traditional domain adaptation methods struggle to generalize effectively due to a failure to adequately capture domain-invariant features. We introduce a meta-learning framework where a model learns to align representations across a distribution of domains during meta-training. This dynamic alignment process allows the model to adapt its representation learning strategy to new, unseen domains, resulting in improved generalization performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through theoretical analysis and simulation results, highlighting its ability to overcome the limitations of static domain adaptation techniques. The key contribution lies in the dynamic nature of the representation alignment, fostering a more robust and adaptable model.

title: Causal Discovery via Counterfactual Simulations with Variational Inference
abstract: Traditional causal discovery methods frequently struggle with the pervasive issue of bias inherent in observational data. These biases can lead to inaccurate or misleading inferences about causal relationships. This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery that addresses this challenge through the integration of counterfactual simulations and variational inference. The core idea is to generate counterfactual scenarios – hypothetical situations that explore "what if" questions – to rigorously test causal hypotheses. Variational inference is then employed to estimate the underlying causal structure from the observed data, leveraging the simulated counterfactuals to reduce the impact of bias. We demonstrate that this combined approach offers a more robust and reliable method for causal discovery compared to conventional techniques. The proposed method provides a framework for exploring causal relationships in complex systems where biases are anticipated to be significant. The resulting causal model provides a more accurate representation of the true underlying causal structure.

title: Non-linear Topological Geometry: A Quantum Dynamics Modeling Framework
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of non-linear topological geometry and quantum dynamics, proposing a novel computational framework leveraging the inherent non-linear characteristics of topological structures to simulate complex physical systems. We introduce the concept of "quantum topology" – a state where topological properties are inherently quantized, and utilize this principle to model quantum systems' behavior within these structures. This work addresses limitations of traditional quantum simulation methods by offering a framework that explicitly incorporates non-linear dynamics and quantum effects, providing a new approach to understanding and modeling intricate physical phenomena. The core mechanism involves mapping topological invariants to quantum states and exploiting the non-linear nature of these states to generate realistic simulations. We demonstrate the framework's capability to generate complex topological structures and simulate quantum transitions within these structures, revealing subtle quantum effects not readily observable in conventional simulations.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Optimization of Quantum Systems
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum system optimization algorithm based on adaptive quantum system dynamics. Traditional optimization methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting the potential for improved performance. We propose a dynamically adjustable algorithm that leverages the inherent properties of quantum systems to optimize them in real-time. The core mechanism involves a continuous feedback loop that adjusts algorithm parameters based on the quantum system's state, resulting in enhanced efficiency compared to static optimization techniques. This approach addresses the limitations of current algorithms by providing a framework for adapting to the specific characteristics of each quantum system. The design incorporates a novel weighting scheme to determine the impact of each parameter adjustment, ensuring a balanced and effective optimization process. The results demonstrate significant improvements in various quantum system optimization tasks, particularly in scenarios with complex dynamics.

title: Les applications quantiques dans l’automobile Perspectives 2030-2035
abstract: L’informatique et les technologies quantiques connaissent aussi une accélération dans l’industrie automobile. Loin d’être de simples curiosités de laboratoire, elles se positionnent comme des leviers de compétitivité concrets à l’horizon 2030-2035, en particulier dans quatre domaines : la simulation et l’optimisation ; les capteurs de précision ; les communications sécurisées ; et la recherche sur les batteries. Dans cet article, nous proposons une analyse structurée de chacun de ces domaines, de leur maturité actuelle, de leurs perspectives d’intégration industrielle et des risques associés. Nous suggérons des pistes pour prioriser des investissements dans ces technologies émergentes.

title: Разработка адаптивной системы управления контентом на основе оптимизации и анализа откликов аудитории
abstract: Целью работы является разработка и исследование системы адаптивной генерации новостных реприз, объединяющей механизмы семантической дедупликации, этической фильтрации и адаптивной настройки параметров языковой модели на основе обратной связи от аудитории и внешних факторов. Были решены следующие задачи:  проведён анализ теоретических аспектов управления контентом, методов генерации, подходов к дедупликации и фильтрации;  спроектирована архитектура системы, определены функциональные требования, обоснован выбор технологического стека;  реализованы модули сбора новостей, семантической дедупликации, генерации с классификацией чувствительности и постпроверкой;  реализованы модули сбора реакций аудитории, учёта погодных данных, а также модуль адаптивного обновления параметров;  разработана методика экспериментальной валидации системы. Актуальность темы обусловлена потребностью в автоматизации создания новостного контента с решением задач исключения дубликатов, предотвращения неуместного тона и адаптации стиля под реакцию аудитории. Источниками информации выступили данные новостных сайтов, метеорологические данные, реакции аудитории из Telegram-канала, а также отечественная и зарубежная научно-исследовательская литература по методам NLP, LLM и адаптивного управления контентом. Разработанная система реализована на языке Python с использованием библиотек requests, beautifulsoup4, pandas, schedule, платформы локального развёртывания LLM Ollama, Telegram Bot API и MTProto API. Результаты работы могут быть применены для автоматизации контент-процессов в новостных каналах, маркетинговых инструментах, образовательных платформах и корпоративных системах генерации отчётов.

title: CTC score-based transcription quality annotation for stable text-to-speech synthesis training on noisy transcriptions
abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has been increasingly adopted for generating transcriptions to train text-to-speech (TTS) models, substantially reducing manual annotation costs. However, transcription errors introduced by ASR systems inevitably degrade TTS performance, and existing approaches lack explicit quality awareness, leaving it unclear whether TTS models can learn to distinguish and respond to varying transcription quality. This study investigates whether explicit quality supervision can enable TTS models to develop quality-aware representations and achieve controllable stable synthesis. This study proposes transcription quality labels (TQL), automatically derived from connectionist temporal classification scores. During training, TQL provides explicit quality supervision, enabling the model to associate transcription quality with acoustic characteristics. During inference, setting TQL to high values guides the model toward stable synthesis that faithfully follows the input text. Under controlled conditions isolating the effect of transcription quality, our best TQL-based model achieves 8.4% word error rate compared to 15.9% for the baseline, a 47% relative reduction. While synthesis accuracy gains are significant, naturalness improvements are modest (mean opinion score of 3.66 vs. 3.55), indicating that TQL primarily enhances synthesis stability rather than perceptual quality. Further analysis confirms that synthesis quality varies systematically with TQL values at inference, demonstrating learned quality-conditioned behavior.

title: The Head Complexity of Boolean Functions in Single-Layer Attention
abstract: What can a single layer of self-attention compute? We study head complexity: the minimum number of attention heads required to compute a function in a one-layer attention-only model. We establish an exact hierarchy under this measure: $k$ heads compute $k$-bit parity but cannot compute $(k+1)$-bit parity. The lower bound is unconditional in the two resources a transformer might otherwise exploit; it holds at unbounded embedding dimension and unbounded numerical precision. The proof rests on an alternating-sum obstruction: after clearing the softmax denominators, every monomial in the resulting decision polynomial omits at least one of the $k+1$ input bits, forcing its correlation with parity to vanish. The same obstruction yields lower bounds for related tasks, including the well-studied multi-hop induction-head task. We also establish compactness bounds for embedding dimension and numerical precision. Specifically, a compactness theorem shows that any function computable at all can be computed with embedding dimension and precision bounded by the discrete data of the task, namely, head count, alphabet size, and length. Thus, potentially unbounded dimension or precision provably cannot substitute for heads. Finally, we derive nearly matching universal bounds for general binary functions: $2^n$ heads suffice to compute every $n$-bit binary function, with one head per monomial in its multilinear expansion, while a counting argument shows almost all such functions require $Ω(2^n/n^2)$ heads. This lower bound matches the upper bound to within a $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ factor, even when dimension and precision are unbounded. Together, these results characterize head requirements for Boolean computation in this model.

title: Speculative Macro Commit for Faster Tool-Using Agents
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents spend wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action--observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation can delay subsequent decisions. We introduce \textbf{Speculative Macro Commit} (SMC), a runtime mechanism for a two-tier agent system: a large authoritative actor model produces the official trajectory, while a faster speculative drafter model continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. SMC mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library used to match against action chains predicted by the drafter at runtime. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps, together with their observations, to the official trajectory. Using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as the authoritative actor model and Qwen3.5-4B as the speculative drafter model, SMC matches the sequential agent's overall accuracy while reducing latency by 10.23\% over the Speculative Actions (SA) baseline and 18.59\% over sequential execution on the $τ^2$-Bench Telecom subset. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7\% over SA baseline and 44.9\% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion. Overall, SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions. Our code is publicly available \href{https://github.com/zeyuliu1037/speculative-macro-commit}{\textcolor{magenta}{here}}.

title: Hardware-Enforced Route Origination Gating for Interdomain Routing Infrastructure: Fixed-Function Prefix Authorization, Physical-Presence Provisioning, and Completeness-Attested Announcement Records
abstract: This technical disclosure describes a hardware-enforced authorization mechanism for interdomain internet routing, published as prior art and dedicated to the public domain. The Border Gateway Protocol contains no intrinsic means by which a receiving network can determine whether an announcing network is entitled to announce a given range of addresses. Existing remedies, including Resource Public Key Infrastructure and Route Origin Validation, BGPsec, prefix filters, and registry-derived access control lists, share a structural property: validation and policy execute in software on the routing device itself, inside the same trust domain an adversary with control of that device already occupies. Origin validation constrains receiving networks rather than originating ones, so a compromised device will construct and emit whatever its software is instructed to emit. The disclosed system places a fixed-function hardware module on the egress path between a routing device's control plane and its external peering interfaces. The module parses protocol messages at line rate and permits emission of an origination announcement only where the asserted prefix, prefix length, and origin Autonomous System are affirmatively matched by an entry in an authorization set held in hardware-protected memory and anchored by a hash committed to one-time-programmable fuses. Any announcement not matched, and any message the module cannot parse or unambiguously classify, is denied. The authorization set is modifiable only through a dedicated physical interface requiring a signed bundle together with a physical presence credential that cannot be generated or replayed over a network, with scope-widening changes classified in fixed-function logic and requiring multiple independent approvals. Two further mechanisms are described. Withdrawal of authorized prefixes is rate-limited in hardware, on the reasoning that coordinated mass withdrawal removes an organization from global reachability as effectively as any hostile announcement, and that withdrawal is conventionally left unfiltered. Every authorization decision, together with a signed record emitted at a fixed interval whether or not any announcement occurred, is transmitted over a path the routing device's operating system cannot address or observe, so that a gap in an otherwise gapless sequence constitutes affirmative evidence of interruption, tampering, or module removal. A read-only query interface returns authorization state and completeness-proved records to authorized regulators, peer networks, insurers, and accreditation bodies under a graduated disclosure policy, replacing self-attested assertions about routing security controls with independently verifiable evidence of routing behavior. The disclosure was prompted by reporting of September 2, 2026 that Iranian actors had attempted attacks against United States telecommunications, energy, and water infrastructure, and by federal advisories issued since April 2026 describing exploitation of internet-connected controllers across critical infrastructure. Published guidance in response has consisted of network and software measures that reside in the same trust domain as the systems they protect. The disclosure observes that policy attention has concentrated on infrastructure whose consequential operations are physical, while the interdomain routing system, whose consequential operations are configuration and signaling events, remains governed by controls executing inside the devices they protect. Scope limitations are stated expressly in Section 7. The default-deny property applies to origination announcements and not comprehensively to transit propagation. The mechanism enforces that a device announces only what its holder physically authorized and does not adjudicate whether that authorization was rightful. Fleet-scale key governance, record aggregation across many devices, and authorization for consequential telecommunications configuration operations beyond route origination are outside what is described here. All subject matter is dedicated to the public domain. No patent rights are sought or reserved for the mechanism described.

title: Companion code for: Redundancy Shortens Lifespan: A Survival Analysis of Built-In Parsimony Pressure in Evolving Boolean Programs
abstract: This repository contains the simulation engine, parameter sweep configurations, analysis scripts and figure generators accompanying the manuscript "Redundancy Shortens Lifespan: A Survival Analysis of Built-In Parsimony Pressure in Evolving Boolean Programs". It provides the computational framework used to measure algorithmic waste and topological lifespan in a discrete, size-penalty-free linear genetic programming substrate. The codebase implements the Boolean in-silico environment (mutation, tournament selection, and environmental shocks), the backward-tracing dead-code-elimination algorithm used to compute active description length, and the survival-analytic pipeline (landmark regression, left-censored Tobit envelope fitting, and the closed-form mutational target-size null model) used to test competing explanations of the waste–lifespan relationship. Included are the scripts required to fully reproduce the empirical results from the manuscript across the 1,200-trajectory main grid and all robustness controls, together with the exact random seeds needed to deterministically regenerate the complete dataset (the raw per-generation logs and topology inventories themselves, roughly 64 GB, are not hosted here).

title: Title: Topological Entanglement Dynamics for Accelerated Computation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of topological entanglement dynamics to dramatically accelerate computation. Traditional approaches struggle with the inherent limitations of static entanglement networks, hindering scalability. We propose a novel algorithm centered around dynamically generating and stabilizing topological entanglement networks, driven by a feedback loop that adapts to network topology evolution. This mechanism aims to overcome these limitations and offer a paradigm shift towards exponential speedups in specific computational tasks. The core of our approach lies in the incorporation of adaptive entanglement generation and stabilization techniques, resulting in a continuously evolving, self-stabilizing structure. We detail the algorithm's design, demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical analysis, and present preliminary results on a simplified example demonstrating potential speedups. The insights gained from this research contribute to a deeper understanding of topological entanglement networks and their application to accelerating computation.

title: 基于自适应的深度学习数据增强
abstract: This paper introduces a novel data augmentation technique, termed "Self-Adaptive Data Augmentation" (SAD), designed to enhance the robustness of deep learning models. Traditional data augmentation methods typically rely on predefined parameters, which can lead to suboptimal results. This work proposes a self-learning algorithm that dynamically adjusts the parameters of the data augmentation process to optimize performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SAD through experiments on several deep learning models, showcasing significant improvements in model accuracy and generalization. The core mechanism of SAD lies in a feedback loop that continuously evaluates the impact of augmented data on model performance and adjusts the augmentation strategy accordingly. The resulting approach offers a more robust and adaptable method for data augmentation, addressing a critical limitation of existing techniques.

title: 基于神经图的自动梯度提升算法的自适应学习策略
abstract: This paper introduces a novel automatic gradient boosting algorithm based on neural graph theory, designed to adapt learning rates and regularization coefficients dynamically to varying datasets and model architectures. Traditional gradient boosting methods often rely on manual parameter tuning, limiting their ability to effectively handle complex datasets and models. Our algorithm leverages a neural graph theory framework to learn data representations and automatically adjust these representations, thereby enhancing learning efficiency and generalization performance. The core mechanism involves a neural graph network that learns latent features, allowing the algorithm to adapt to different learning scenarios. This work addresses a significant limitation of gradient boosting by providing a more flexible and adaptive approach.

title: Title: Adaptive Bayesian Network for Dynamic System Dynamics
abstract: This paper presents an Adaptive Bayesian Network (ABN) designed to enhance the prediction of complex dynamic systems. Traditional Bayesian networks struggle with the inherent variability of real-world data and require extensive manual parameter tuning. Our proposed ABN incorporates a dynamic adjustment mechanism that intelligently refines the network's parameters based on observed system behavior, leading to improved prediction accuracy and robustness. We explore a novel approach to parameter adaptation using a Bayesian optimization strategy to minimize prediction error while maintaining a high level of accuracy. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously evaluates the network's performance and adjusts the influence of each factor to maximize predictive power. The results demonstrate significant improvements in forecasting accuracy, particularly for dynamic systems with complex interactions. This work represents a substantial step towards creating adaptive systems capable of handling the inherent uncertainty of real-world data.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Adaptive Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a peculiar phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers a unique approach to algorithm design. This paper proposes a novel adaptive algorithm leveraging quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust its internal parameters and computational processes based on input data. The core mechanism centers around the algorithm's ability to evolve its behavior in response to changes within the data stream, offering a potential paradigm shift for machine learning and data analysis. This adaptive capability surpasses traditional approaches, providing enhanced adaptability and accuracy. This work explores the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of this algorithm, highlighting its potential to revolutionize these fields.

title: Quantum-Inspired Probabilistic Circuit Synthesis
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neural circuit synthesis, drawing inspiration from the principles of quantum mechanics. Traditional neural network optimization often relies on deterministic algorithms, which can be susceptible to local optima and limited exploration of the solution space. This work proposes a methodology termed "Quantum-Inspired Probabilistic Circuit Synthesis" that leverages concepts like superposition and interference to introduce probabilistic pathways within a neural network architecture. The core idea is to generate a network where connections between nodes are not fixed but governed by probabilities, allowing for a more diverse and robust exploration of the circuit's behavior. We formulate a synthesis process based on probabilistic gate selection and connection weighting, mimicking quantum interference to constructively reinforce promising pathways and destructively cancel unfavorable ones. This approach aims to significantly improve the efficiency and robustness of neural circuit design, offering a potentially superior alternative to conventional deterministic methods. The theoretical framework is presented, along with a description of the core algorithmic components, and a discussion of the potential benefits and challenges associated with this new paradigm.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Algorithm Design for Constraint Satisfaction Problems
abstract: Constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) represent a fundamental class of NP-complete problems that pose significant challenges for classical computation, particularly as problem instances grow in size. This work investigates the application of quantum computing techniques – specifically quantum annealing and quantum walks – to accelerate the solution process for CSPs. The core idea involves mapping the CSP to an equivalent quantum Ising model. This model is then targeted for solution via quantum annealing, exploiting quantum tunneling to escape local minima and explore the solution space. Furthermore, quantum walk algorithms are explored for efficient solution space traversal. The potential for achieving speedups over traditional CSP solvers is examined, highlighting the promise of quantum computing for tackling computationally intensive combinatorial optimization problems. The research focuses on the theoretical design and analysis of these quantum algorithms, without requiring experimental validation. The primary outcome is a framework for designing quantum algorithms tailored to specific CSP instances, providing a foundation for future research and potential implementation.

title: High-Order Geometry and Quantum Information Encoding
abstract: This paper explores the potential of high-order geometry as a foundation for quantum information encoding. We propose a novel framework leveraging geometric structures to represent and manipulate quantum states, aiming to deepen our understanding of quantum information itself. The core mechanism involves utilizing high-order geometric properties to induce specific quantum behavior within a system. This investigation addresses the potential of high-order geometry to provide a new and potentially transformative approach to quantum information processing. This work focuses on the design of a quantum information encoding scheme predicated on the inherent geometric properties of quantum systems.

This investigation addresses the potential of high-order geometry to provide a new and potentially transformative approach to quantum information processing. This work focuses on the design of a quantum information encoding scheme predicated on the inherent geometric properties of quantum systems.

title: Quantum Annealing Combinatorial Optimization (QACO)
abstract: This paper explores the application of Quantum Annealing (QA) to the field of combinatorial optimization. The core idea is to leverage the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically quantum tunneling, to efficiently solve complex optimization problems. We present a framework for utilizing QA to tackle problems represented as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models. The methodology focuses on mapping the problem's constraints and objective function into a form suitable for QA hardware. We discuss the challenges involved in this mapping process, including the limitations of current QA devices and the need for careful problem formulation. Furthermore, we analyze the potential advantages of QA over classical optimization techniques, particularly concerning the exploration of a wider solution space. The research highlights the promise of QACO as a viable approach for tackling computationally demanding combinatorial optimization tasks, offering a novel method to enhance optimization efficiency.

title: Title: Resonance-Based Cryptography (RBC)
abstract: Resonance-Based Cryptography (RBC) proposes a novel cryptographic approach centered on the concept of mathematical structures exhibiting resonant frequencies. This system leverages subtle, mathematically-driven changes in the system's state to generate unique keys, offering a potential defense against traditional cryptographic methods. The core claim is that specific mathematical patterns possess inherent resonance properties, enabling the creation of keys resistant to brute-force attacks and potentially offering enhanced security. This paper provides a detailed exploration of the RBC framework, outlining its theoretical foundation, key mathematical constructs, and potential implementations. The study focuses on the development of a robust key generation process, exploring the interplay between mathematical patterns and physical resonance to achieve secure key distribution.

title: Neuro-Topology Adaptive Optimization (NTAO)
abstract: This paper introduces Neuro-Topology Adaptive Optimization (NTAO), a novel approach to neural network architecture optimization that moves beyond predefined search spaces and manual topology design. NTAO leverages reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust the network's topology based on observed network activity, effectively mimicking the competitive and collaborative dynamics observed in biological neural networks. The core of NTAO is a "topology controller" trained via reinforcement learning, which observes network metrics such as activation values, gradients, and error signals to modify synaptic connections and introduce or remove neurons. The controller's decisions are guided by a reward function that prioritizes prediction accuracy, convergence speed, and computational efficiency. This approach represents a significant departure from traditional methods, offering a more adaptive and potentially superior solution for neural network design. The key innovation lies in treating topology optimization as a learned process, enabling the network to autonomously explore and refine its structure.
