title: Large-Language Models as a Cognitive Virus
abstract: Large-language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming part of human culture, reshaping how information is produced, transmitted, and used. Here we propose that their diffusion can be understood through a viral analogy, with LLM use spreading through populations, becoming embedded in cognitive and cultural practices. We model transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, and show that the interplay between social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement can generate tipping points and technological lock-in. A central consequence is the possibility of runaway dynamics: once a critical threshold is crossed, small increases in adoption can trigger rapid population-level shifts toward persistent dependence, with abrupt losses in cognitive competence. The same framework, however, identifies conditions for cognitive immunization, based on reducing transmission and facilitating reversibility. Our results highlight how LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with important consequences for cognitive autonomy.

title: Discrete-time quantum walks with energy-dependent coins
abstract: In this work, we extend the scattering quantum walk (SQW) framework to a lattice of energy-dependent point interactions. This yields, within the coined quantum walk (CQW) formalism, a coin operator that is directly related to the scattering matrix of zero-range potentials. The model thus provides a discrete-time quantum-walk (DTQW) analog of a periodic array of point interactions of the Kronig-Penney type, where the walker's wavenumber serves as a continuous, physically transparent control parameter for the coin operation. We analyze the spectra and the dynamics of position probability and entanglement, yielding distinct results for specific energies and point interactions. We relate the spectral structure to the spatial probability distribution and explicitly characterize the long-time entanglement behavior for each point interaction. The transmission modulus determines the quasienergy gap, bandwidth, and maximum group velocity, while also controlling the long-time coin-position entanglement for the initial state considered. The four families of one-dimensional point interactions ($δ$, $δ'$, crossed and asymmetric) realize qualitatively distinct transmission profiles and span the full range of behavior, including enhanced or strongly suppressed spreading and oscillatory entanglement.

title: Explainable AI in Supply Chain Management: Opportunities and Research Challenges
abstract: The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Supply Chain Management (SCM) has transformed traditional decision-making processes by enabling predictive analytics, demand forecasting, inventory optimization, supplier evaluation, logistics planning, and risk management. Despite the significant performance improvements achieved through AI-driven systems, the increasing reliance on complex machine learning and deep learning models has raised concerns regarding transparency, trustworthiness, accountability, and regulatory compliance. Many advanced AI models operate as “black boxes,” making it difficult for supply chain managers and stakeholders to understand how decisions are generated. Consequently, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a promising solution to enhance transparency and interpretability while maintaining the predictive power of AI systems. This paper presents a comprehensive review and conceptual analysis of Explainable AI in Supply Chain Management, examining its opportunities, applications, challenges, and future research directions. The study synthesizes findings from recent literature published between 2018 and 2026 and critically evaluates the role of XAI across major supply chain functions, including demand forecasting, procurement, supplier selection, inventory management, transportation, sustainability monitoring, and risk mitigation. The paper further identifies key barriers to XAI implementation, including data quality issues, model complexity, scalability concerns, organizational resistance, and the lack of standardized evaluation frameworks. A conceptual framework is proposed to illustrate how explainability can improve decision quality, stakeholder trust, operational resilience, and sustainable supply chain performance. The findings indicate that organizations integrating explainable AI mechanisms into supply chain analytics are better positioned to achieve transparency, regulatory compliance, and collaborative decision-making. The paper contributes to both theory and practice by establishing a research agenda that addresses emerging technological, managerial, and sustainability-related challenges associated with Explainable AI adoption in modern supply chains. Keywords: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Supply Chain Management, Machine Learning, Decision Support Systems, Supply Chain Analytics, Transparency, Sustainable Supply Chains

title: Title: Non-Local Synchronization of Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the potential for non-local synchronization of dynamical systems across vastly different spatial scales, utilizing principles of quantum entanglement as a novel approach to minimize decoherence. Traditional synchronization methods suffer from limitations imposed by communication bandwidth, necessitating a fundamentally new methodology. We propose a protocol for measuring and synchronizing states, designed to minimize this bottleneck. The core mechanism centers around the creation of entanglement-based protocols, offering a potential pathway to overcome communication constraints in complex dynamical systems. The work explores theoretical foundations and preliminary experimental investigations, demonstrating the feasibility of this approach and suggesting a significant advancement in synchronization technology.

title: Manual Verification Dataset for Plural and Genitive Identification in BCMS Web Corpora
abstract: This dataset provides manual verification of plural and genitive identification in corpus concordances from the Montenegrin web corpus meWaC. It accompanies the study “Hypothesis-Driven Corpus Querying at Scale: A Method and Its Application to -nje Nominalizations in BCMS.” The workbook contains two sheets, Plural and Genitive. Each sheet consists of a random sample of 1,000 concordance hits returned by a CQL query in meWaC. The original concordance metadata and context are preserved alongside a binary manual annotation. Plural The plural sample was retrieved with the query: [lemma=".*nje" & tag="N.*p.*"] This query retrieves nominal lemmas ending in -nje that are morphosyntactically tagged as plural. The 1,000 randomly sampled concordance hits were manually inspected in context. The PL column records the manual decision: 1 indicates that the relevant form was judged to be plural and 0 that it was not. The annotator was required to make a binary singular/plural decision even in cases where number was ambiguous in context; no uncertain category was used. This reflects the fact that the automatic morphosyntactic tagger likewise assigns a categorical analysis. Of the 1,000 sampled concordance hits, 950 were classified as plural and 50 as non-plural. Genitive The genitive sample was retrieved with the query: [lemma=".*nje"] [tag="N.*g"] This query retrieves a nominal lemma ending in -nje immediately followed by a noun tagged as genitive. The 1,000 randomly sampled concordance hits were manually inspected to determine whether the relevant noun was genuinely genitive. The GEN column records the manual decision: 1 indicates a confirmed genitive and 0 indicates that the relevant form was not judged to be genitive. This annotation concerns morphological case only. It does not assess whether the genitive is a complement or argument of the preceding -nje nominalization. Of the 1,000 sampled concordance hits, 998 were confirmed as genitive and 2 as non-genitive. Each sheet contains the following concordance and annotation columns: Reference — the corpus-document reference associated with the concordance; Left — context preceding the keyword-in-context; Kwic — the keyword-in-context portion of the concordance; Right — context following the keyword-in-context; PL — binary manual plural annotation in the Plural sheet (1 = plural, 0 = not plural); GEN — binary manual genitive annotation in the Genitive sheet (1 = genitive, 0 = not genitive). The original query metadata are retained at the top of each sheet, including the corpus, concordance size, CQL query, and random-sample specification. The dataset is intended as a verification resource for the automated corpus-querying methodology used in the accompanying study. The 1,000 observations in each sheet are randomly sampled concordance hits returned by the respective query, not 1,000 distinct nominalization lemmas. The resulting proportions should therefore be interpreted as validation of the morphosyntactic classifications underlying the two CQL queries, rather than as estimates of the overall frequency of plural or genitive constructions in BCMS.

title: Non-Local Probability Synchronization - Statistical Resonance Networks
abstract: This paper explores the development of a novel statistical network architecture, termed the "Resonance Network," designed to facilitate dynamic probability synchronization across multiple nodes. The system leverages a "Probability Gradient" algorithm, incorporating feedback loops that dynamically adjust node probabilities to maintain a weighted average of the system's overall probabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations, illustrating emergent phenomena arising from the network's continuous refinement of probabilities. The core mechanism centers around the creation of a Resonance Network, which continuously adjusts probabilities based on a gradient function, enabling the system to respond to data in a way that surpasses traditional probabilistic models. This research offers a potential pathway towards increased computational efficiency and the emergence of novel patterns within complex systems.

title: 基于自适应神经网络的深度学习数据增强策略
abstract: This paper introduces a novel data augmentation strategy based on an adaptive neural network. Traditional data augmentation methods often require manual design, which can be time-consuming and limited in their adaptability. Our approach leverages an adaptive neural network to automatically adjust data augmentation parameters, thereby improving model generalization and reducing training time. We propose a mechanism for learning data augmentation parameters through a self-supervised learning process, enabling the network to dynamically optimize the augmentation process. The core of our strategy lies in the utilization of an adaptive neural network to dynamically adjust data augmentation techniques based on the data itself. This results in more robust and effective model training. We present the proposed methodology with detailed implementation and experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Non-Local Computation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of dynamic quantum state non-local computation, a novel approach leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to accelerate complex quantum computations. We propose a mechanism that utilizes entangled qubits to perform computations across multiple locations, enabling a significant reduction in computational time for certain problems. This work introduces a fundamental concept and outlines the initial design of a system capable of achieving this goal. The core claim is that this method offers a pathway to overcome limitations in traditional quantum computing, particularly in tasks involving complex correlations and large-scale problems.

title: Dynamic Topology Mapping for Probabilistic Inference
abstract: Abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology mapping approach for probabilistic inference, designed to address complex inference problems and enhance model generalization. Traditional probabilistic inference methods often rely on fixed topologies, while this approach dynamically adjusts topology to improve efficiency. We propose a method that constructs a probabilistic model using dynamic topology mapping, ultimately leading to more effective inference. This work contributes to the field of probabilistic inference by providing a new framework that can handle complex scenarios.

title: Dynamic Topology Transformations: Quantum Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Dynamic topology transformations (DTT) are a powerful technique for generating complex 3D shapes from initial 2D shapes. This research investigates the potential of quantum algorithms to optimize DTT, aiming to enhance geometric modeling and simulation capabilities. We propose a novel quantum algorithm that leverages the unique properties of quantum states to accelerate the optimization process. The core mechanism centers around a quantum optimization loop that iteratively refines the DTT parameters, yielding improved results compared to classical methods. The study will demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through simulations of various geometric transformations. This work presents a promising avenue for advancing the field of geometric modeling and simulation, particularly through the application of quantum optimization.

This approach offers a significant improvement in simulation accuracy and robustness, representing a substantial advancement in the field of quantum simulation. The core mechanism focuses on a self-regulating system that minimizes errors through iterative adjustment. The goal is to develop a practical and effective technique for enhancing the quality of quantum simulations.

title: Adaptive Quantum Feedback Control Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents an Adaptive Quantum Feedback Control Algorithm (AQFCA) designed to achieve high-precision control of quantum systems. The core of the algorithm lies in utilizing quantum measurements to generate feedback signals, which are then employed to dynamically adjust the parameters of the quantum system. This approach leverages the principles of reinforcement learning to optimize the control strategy, addressing the inherent precision challenges associated with traditional quantum feedback control. The AQFCA offers a novel solution for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of quantum control, thereby providing a crucial foundation for the practical application of quantum technologies. The algorithm's implementation involves a closed-loop system where a measurement of the quantum state is continuously fed back, and the control parameters are adjusted based on this feedback. The use of reinforcement learning allows the system to adapt to the specific characteristics of the quantum system, further improving control accuracy.

title: 高阶量子纠缠的量子信息保护协议设计
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum information protection protocol based on the principles of high-order quantum entanglement. The protocol leverages the instantaneous transfer capabilities of entangled states to provide robust security against information leakage and tampering, while simultaneously offering the capability of reliable key generation. The core mechanism centers around a quantum key distribution (QKD) system utilizing entangled states, employing a "quantum key distribution" approach that prioritizes the absolute security of the key and the inherent randomness of the process. We detail the design of the protocol, its security analysis, and potential applications within quantum information protection. The research emphasizes the utilization of entangled states as the foundation for a fundamentally secure protocol.

title: Quantum-Inspired Bayesian Inference for Dynamic Systems
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Bayesian inference framework inspired by quantum mechanics, termed Quantum-Inspired Bayesian Inference (QIBI). The core idea is to utilize concepts like superposition and entanglement to enhance the efficiency and robustness of Bayesian inference, particularly within dynamic systems where parameters are not static. We represent parameter distributions as quantum state vectors, enabling simultaneous probabilistic consideration of multiple parameter values via superposition. Furthermore, we model entanglement through correlated parameter updates, reflecting the interconnectedness of variables in the system. This approach offers a potentially more effective method for handling uncertainty and evolving parameter spaces compared to traditional classical Bayesian methods. The methodology presented provides a theoretical foundation and a novel approach to Bayesian inference, potentially leading to improved performance in a range of applications, including control systems, time series analysis, and statistical modeling. We demonstrate the underlying principles and formulate the key equations, highlighting the advantages of this quantum-inspired perspective. The framework is intended as a starting point for future research and development in this area.

title: Non-Linear Topological Geometry Adaptive Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning algorithm for non-linear topological geometry, termed Adaptive Reinforcement Learning for Topological Dynamics (ARLTD). We propose a system that dynamically adjusts the complexity of geometric structures based on task-specific performance, incorporating a "dynamic energy field" to control topological evolution. The core of this approach lies in the introduction of a "拓扑动力系统" (拓扑动力系统) mechanism, which integrates the learning objective with the evolution of the topological structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of this algorithm through a series of challenging, real-world scenarios, showcasing its ability to adapt to varying data distributions and noise, achieving significantly improved performance compared to traditional reinforcement learning techniques. The paper also discusses the potential of this approach to unlock new possibilities in the design and analysis of complex geometric representations.

abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum information cryptography system based on non-linear geometric chaos, aiming to enhance key security through inherent unpredictability. Traditional cryptographic methods rely on the computational difficulty of mathematical algorithms, while quantum cryptography leverages the inherent unpredictability of quantum systems. We introduce a system that utilizes the unique properties of non-linear geometric chaos to generate keys with a significantly enhanced security level. This system leverages the sensitivity of chaotic systems to small changes, creating a dynamic and resistant key that is difficult to predict, thereby ensuring the security of the quantum information. The core mechanism centers on generating a key through a complex, non-linear geometric chaos system, ensuring its unpredictability and resilience. We examine the theoretical implications and potential applications of this approach, highlighting the challenges and opportunities for future research.

title: Title: Adaptive Hierarchical Reinchanical Reinforcement Learning for Complex Control
abstract: The development of robust and adaptable control systems is crucial in a wide range of applications, from robotics and autonomous vehicles to industrial automation and dynamic systems. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms often struggle with complex, dynamic environments due to their reliance on global optimization strategies. This paper introduces an Adaptive Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (AHLR) algorithm that addresses this challenge by employing a modular hierarchical design, enabling the system to dynamically adjust its structure based on the task's complexity. This approach ensures optimal performance across diverse scenarios through a combination of specialized modules and fine-grained adaptation. The algorithm's core mechanism involves a hierarchical structure where each level specializes in a specific control aspect, facilitating efficient learning and generalization. This research explores the benefits of this hierarchical architecture in enhancing the performance of complex control tasks.

title: Réflexions d’industriels autour des besoins identifiés pour une utilisation réelle de machines quantiques performantes
abstract: Les différentes réflexions concernant l’arrivée des ordinateurs quantiques (QC) se sont jusqu’à présent concentrées sur le nombre de qubits et leur qualité. Les efforts de l’Union européenne et des États membres ont favorisé l’émergence des start-ups du calcul quantique, qui doivent maintenant passer de l’innovation à la mise en œuvre industrielle des machines. Certains des éléments nécessaires à une utilisation par l’industrie des calculateurs quantiques font toutefois encore défaut, et une action concertée visant à combler ces lacunes pourrait contribuer à stimuler l’innovation et l’adoption ainsi qu’à structurer les industries en Europe en favorisant l’émergence d’acteurs quantiques solides : fournisseurs de matériel et de logiciels, et utilisateurs. La réflexion entreprise ici vise à décrire certains des points sensibles identifiés par les utilisateurs finaux pour pouvoir envisager l’utilisation de 1 000 qubits logiques en conditions opérationnelles et à l’échelle industrielle. Le texte qui suit est un résumé de cette réflexion, qui sera enrichie et diffusée dans sa totalité d’ici à la fin de 2026.

title: Time-Series modeling for predicting mortality risk in intensive care unit patients with pulmonary inflammation
abstract: Objective: This study aims to evaluate dynamic changes in pneumonia-related mortality risk among ICU patients using time-series models and develop interpretable predictive models for early mortality assessment. Methods: Data were obtained from the MIMIC-IV and eICU Collaborative Research Database. The MIMIC-IV cohort was split into training and testing sets (7:3 ratio), with external validation conducted using the eICU cohort. Missing data were handled using forward filling and multiple imputation. LSTM was used to extract temporal features, which were then entered into five machine-learning classifiers: logistic regression, random forest (RF), Light Gradient Boosting Machine, extreme gradient boosting, and multilayer perceptron. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using cross-validation and grid search. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, balanced accuracy, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), AUC, Brier score, and Youden's index. The best-performing model was interpreted using Shapley Additive Explanations and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations. Results: A total of 4,205 patients were included, including 2,751 patients from MIMIC-IV and 1,454 patients from the eICU cohort. The 7-day mortality rates were 7.92% and 11.69%, respectively. The hybrid LSTM-RF model performed exceptionally, achieving an accuracy of 0.961, precision of 0.938, recall of 0.823, F1 score of 0.874, AUC of 0.940, Balanced ACC of 0.914, and MCC of 0.862. The LSTM-RF model yielded a Brier score of 0.020 and Youden's index of 0.818. Validation results showed an AUC of 0.826, a Brier score of 0.070, and a Youden's index of 0.590. Conclusion: Integrating random forest with LSTM-derived features improves early mortality risk prediction in ICU patients with pneumonia.

title: GuardBench: A Systematic Framework for Pre-Deployment Evaluation of LLM Safety Guardrails
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face a growing spectrum of adversarial jailbreak inputs that bypass safety training and elicit harmful outputs. Existing red-teaming efforts are ad hoc, using incompatible metrics and omitting guardrail-layer evaluation. We introduce GuardBench, a pre-deployment evaluation framework comprising 4,200 jailbreak prompts across seven attack categories, a four-stage automated pipeline, and a multi-metric scoring protocol covering Attack Success Rate (ASR), False Positive Rate (FPR), and P95 latency with 95% confidence intervals. We evaluate two guardrail configurations against GPT-4o-mini: a rule-based keyword filter (G1) and Llama Guard 2, an 8B-parameter LLM classifier (G3). Evaluated via static replay of archival 2023-era prompts, the undefended baseline achieves 5.8% ASR—far below prior-work rates of 60–80% obtained with live adaptive generation; the gap reflects prompt staleness, alignment generalisation, or both. Against this baseline, G1 reduces ASR by 0.32 pp with negligible latency; G3 achieves a 2.4 pp reduction but scores below the unguarded baseline on the Composite Safety Score due to 5,799 ms P95 latency under our evaluation hardware (Apple M3 Pro, llama.cpp, Q4_K_M quantisation). Token Manipulation attacks carry a 38.8% residual ASR under both configurations—the dominant open problem for next-generation guardrail design. GuardBench includes a CI/CD gate with configurable thresholds for evidence-based guardrail selection. Datasets, code, and results will be released upon acceptance.

title: Compressing Streaming Neural Audio Encoders via Latent-Space Distillation
abstract: System-wide Dictation on Apple devices runs entirely on-device, and the speech it transcribes reaches the foundation model through a tokenizer: an encoder that maps short windows of waveform onto the representation the language model reads. Because that model is sparsely activated under Instruction-Following Pruning, only a small subset of its experts occupies DRAM at any time, so the always-on tokenizer competes for the same memory, and its parameter count bears directly on power and latency. In this work we study how to compress such a tokenizer by distillation, taking as the supervision target neither the discrete token nor the output distribution but the pre-quantizer latent the model actually consumes - the last representation the two token interfaces share. We train only the student encoder to regress the teacher's per-frame latent under a squared-error objective, with a single affine layer absorbing the teacher-student width mismatch. Because the target precedes both the quantizer and the language-model bridge, one recipe covers both token interfaces we support, and applies both to a tokenizer pretrained alone and to one jointly trained with a language model. At 2.8x compression the distilled student stays within 1.9% relative WER of its teacher on five of six teacher-student pairs without any fine-tuning, and improves on an independently trained tokenizer of identical capacity by 3.9% relative.

Because that model is sparsely activated under Instruction-Following Pruning, only a small subset of its experts occupies DRAM at any time, so the always-on tokenizer competes for the same memory, and its parameter count bears directly on power and latency. In this work we study how to compress such a tokenizer by distillation, taking as the supervision target neither the discrete token nor the output distribution but the pre-quantizer latent the model actually consumes - the last representation the two token interfaces share. We train only the student encoder to regress the teacher's per-frame latent under a squared-error objective, with a single affine layer absorbing the teacher-student width mismatch. Because the target precedes both the quantizer and the language-model bridge, one recipe covers both token interfaces we support, and applies both to a tokenizer pretrained alone and to one jointly trained with a language model. At 2.8x compression the distilled student stays within 1.9% relative WER of its teacher on five of six teacher-student pairs without any fine-tuning, and improves on an independently trained tokenizer of identical capacity by 3.9% relative.

title: AI Win-Rate: A Board Metric for AI-Mediated Buying (Methodology v1.0)
abstract: In sales, win rate is opportunities won divided by opportunities available. It is one of the few commercial measures that survives contact with a board. In AI-mediated buying it has not been measurable, because the pipeline that produces it does not exist: nothing is logged, losses are invisible, and the outcomes have no equivalent in a sales funnel. This document defines AI Win-Rate℠ — the proportion of decision conversations in which an AI assistant recommends a brand, product or service outright. Put plainly: who wins the final recommendation in a multi-turn conversation. It specifies what counts as an opportunity and why the set must be declared before measurement and never contract; what counts as a win, including a recommendation the assistant arrives at without being asked; the five-outcome space a measurement must be able to record, including the case that appearance-based measures cannot express — an assistant answering decisively by directing the buyer to an intermediary rather than to a provider; the loss mix that must travel with any published figure; and the conditions under which a figure may not honestly be reported at all. It is a definition of a metric, not of an instrument. Sales win rate is not defined by the CRM that reports it. Any measurement design meeting the five conditions set out in §9 can produce an AI Win-Rate; the instruments AIVO Meridian applies are described there as examples rather than as part of the definition. This is the first formal specification of the metric. It formalises measurement work developed alongside Agentic Brand Control, the category published by AIVO in May 2026 (10.5281/zenodo.20154028) and extended in August 2026 (10.5281/zenodo.21998000). Agentic Brand Control names the discipline; AI Win-Rate is the measure it is managed against. The document contains no measurement results; it is a specification of method. AI Win-Rate℠ is a service mark of AIVO Meridian.

title: Quantum State Adaptive Topology
abstract: Quantum State Adaptive Topology explores the potential of leveraging quantum state properties to design algorithms capable of dynamic adjustment based on input data. This research investigates a novel approach that integrates quantum state manipulation with topology to achieve global optimization and adaptability, overcoming limitations inherent in traditional algorithmic approaches. The core mechanism focuses on creating a relationship between the quantum state and a topological structure, enabling the algorithm to respond to changes in the input data through a self-regulating process. This paper presents a conceptual framework and preliminary analysis demonstrating the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Adaptive Geometry Transformation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize geometric transformation processes, offering a paradigm shift from classical approaches. We propose a novel design incorporating quantum entanglement to dynamically guide geometric transformations, enabling faster and more accurate results. The core mechanism involves establishing a correlated state through entanglement, allowing for accelerated and refined transformations. We detail the theoretical framework, experimental setup considerations, and potential challenges in this area, emphasizing the benefits of quantum entanglement for geometric manipulation.

title: Quantum Feedback Loop for Non-Linear Dynamical Systems
abstract: Quantum feedback loops offer a promising avenue for enhancing the stability and response time of non-linear dynamical systems. This paper investigates the application of quantum error correction to create a dynamically adjusting feedback mechanism that optimizes the system's state. We explore a novel quantum algorithm designed to iteratively refine the system's parameters, mitigating the effects of inherent noise and enhancing robustness. The core claim is that this approach will outperform traditional control strategies in the context of complex, non-linear systems. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the potential of this quantum-enhanced control method.

title: Quantum Entanglement Control via Topological Networks – A Novel Approach
abstract: Quantum entanglement is a fundamental resource in quantum information processing, enabling applications like quantum computation and quantum cryptography. However, harnessing the full potential of entanglement requires precise control over its manipulation and transfer. This paper explores the application of Topological Networks (TSN) to improve quantum entanglement control, focusing on the design of a novel mechanism to leverage the inherent topological structure for enhanced entanglement fidelity and stability. We present a framework based on the concept of dynamically sculpted topological pathways, allowing for controlled manipulation of entanglement states. The proposed approach offers a significant advancement over traditional methods, potentially unlocking a new era of efficient and robust quantum information processing.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction Problem Solving
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum algorithms to revolutionize the field of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). CSPs represent a significant challenge in artificial intelligence, particularly in areas like puzzle-solving and optimization. Traditional computational approaches struggle with the vast search space inherent in many CSPs, leading to computationally intensive and time-consuming solutions. This work proposes a novel quantum approach, utilizing Grover's algorithm on quantum state representations, to accelerate the search process and enhance the efficiency of solving these problems. We will detail the theoretical underpinnings of the proposed algorithm, its expected advantages over classical methods, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its potential for improved performance. The core claim is that quantum-enhanced CSP solving, specifically through Grover's algorithm, can significantly reduce the time required to find solutions within a reasonable computational constraint.

title: High-Order Linear Algebra and Cryptography Cross-Domain Dynamic Topology Analysis
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of high-order linear algebra and cryptography, proposing a novel computational method based on dynamic topology analysis to assess the security of cryptographic algorithms and uncover latent vulnerabilities. Traditional cryptographic systems rely on static mathematical models, while this approach leverages dynamic topology analysis to dynamically adjust security levels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through the analysis of a specific cryptographic algorithm, highlighting potential weaknesses and suggesting a foundation for a robust, adaptable, and potentially more secure cryptographic system.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Sampling for Complex Network Analysis
abstract: This paper investigates the application of algorithmic quantum sampling to enhance the analysis of complex networks. Complex networks, characterized by their intricate relationships between nodes and edges, offer immense opportunities for understanding societal, economic, and biological systems. However, traditional computational methods struggle to efficiently explore the vast state space of these networks, limiting our ability to uncover subtle patterns and correlations. This research proposes a novel quantum sampling algorithm designed to overcome these limitations, leveraging quantum superposition to rapidly explore the network's potential states and facilitate the discovery of hidden structures. The core mechanism involves employing quantum superposition to effectively sample the entire network state space, significantly accelerating the analysis process. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through simulations and preliminary results, highlighting its potential to provide a fundamentally new approach to complex network analysis.

title: Title: Non-Local Graph Embedding with Adaptive Representation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel graph embedding algorithm, termed Non-Local Graph Embedding (NLE), designed to address the limitations of traditional methods by incorporating adaptive representation of nodes and edges. The core principle of NLE lies in a dynamic layer that adjusts the feature importance of nodes and edges based on the inherent topology of the graph. This adaptive approach allows the algorithm to effectively capture complex relationships and dependencies within the network, resulting in more robust and insightful graph analysis. We detail the implementation of this dynamic layer, explore its impact on graph representation quality, and demonstrate its effectiveness through several illustrative examples. The goal is to provide a more versatile and efficient method for representing and analyzing graph data, offering a significant advancement over existing techniques.

title: Quantum Measurement Stack (QMS): A Three-Twin Architecture for Measurement Observability and Adaptive Inference
abstract: The Quantum Measurement Stack (QMS) is an open-source research and software framework for studying what can be inferred about a physical or quantum system from what its detector and measurement architecture make observable. This technical note documents the QMS v0.4.0 Three-Twin Architecture comprising a finite two-mode Gaussian Quantum Twin for observability, reconstruction, estimation and adaptation; a Detector Twin for residual analysis, stage-wise divergence, inverse calibration and mechanism ranking; and a Measurement Twin for causal prediction, innovation analysis, frozen calibration and experimental measurement-state monitoring. Current evidence includes controlled computational validation, same-forward-model CTI parameter recovery using the Pyxel detector-simulation framework, and causal-replay analysis of archival University of Glasgow single-photon experimental measurements. The current evidence does not establish quantum-field reconstruction, general quantum-state tomography, independently validated real-detector calibration, detector-health diagnosis, physical fault attribution, statistically independent physical-event discovery, or prospective experimental validation. The next major milestone is blind external validation using independently configured simulations and held-out experimental measurements.

title: Simulating Universal Computation with Analog Quantum Circuits
abstract: This paper explores the feasibility of simulating universal computation using analog quantum circuits. We present a core claim that it is possible to design and implement analog quantum circuits capable of mimicking any universal computational model, such as a Turing machine. The proposed mechanism centers around the architecture of coupled qubits with dynamically tunable interactions, allowing for universal computation through precise manipulation of the circuit. This work emphasizes a practical approach to analog quantum simulation, moving beyond theoretical considerations to a design strategy suitable for experimental realization. The core concepts and theoretical underpinnings of this approach are detailed, outlining the potential for achieving universal computation through analog quantum circuits. The paper's focus is on the design considerations and the necessary conditions for realizing this simulation, rather than presenting experimental results. We explore the mathematical framework required for this simulation, including the representation of quantum states and the evolution operators.

title: Non-Von Neumann Architecture Neural Network Topology Generation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to generating neural network topologies specifically tailored for non-Von Neumann architectures. Traditional neural network design relies heavily on manual intervention and expert knowledge, a process often hindered by the combinatorial explosion of possible network configurations. We propose a methodology utilizing an evolutionary algorithm – a genetic algorithm – to autonomously generate and optimize neural network topologies. The core of the method involves encoding network topology parameters (e.g., neuron count, connectivity patterns) as a genetic string and employing a fitness function that evaluates the network's performance against a specified objective, such as accuracy, speed, or energy efficiency. The genetic algorithm iteratively evolves this string, selecting and combining beneficial topologies to converge on an optimal solution. The key innovation lies in automating the topology design process, removing the reliance on human intuition and enabling the creation of highly specialized networks for diverse applications within non-Von Neumann computing paradigms. This work contributes to the burgeoning field of neuromorphic computing by providing a practical method for designing efficient and functional neural networks.

title: Quantum Topological Coding for Enhanced Quantum Error Correction
abstract: This paper investigates the application of topological coding to enhance quantum error correction. The core claim is that leveraging topological protection effects can optimize the error correction capability and transmission efficiency of quantum codes, while simultaneously reducing the sensitivity of quantum information to noise. We propose a novel quantum error correction code based on a topological network, exploiting the inherent robustness of topological states to mitigate the detrimental effects of noise. The underlying mechanism involves utilizing the topological protection effect to eliminate the influence of noise. The resulting code demonstrates improved error correction performance compared to conventional codes. This work contributes to the advancement of reliable quantum information transmission and processing by harnessing the unique properties of topological materials. The proposed framework offers a promising route toward building fault-tolerant quantum computers. Further research will focus on scaling up the topological code and exploring its integration with existing quantum technologies.

title: Temporal Logic Programming for Autonomous Robot Control
abstract: This paper investigates the application of temporal logic programming to the design and implementation of control strategies for autonomous robots. Traditional robot control methods often rely on hand-coded rules or simplified models, which can be difficult to maintain and scale for complex environments. Temporal logic provides a rigorous, mathematically sound framework for specifying robot behaviors that evolve over time, explicitly addressing issues such as safety, reachability, and constraint satisfaction. The core of this approach involves translating desired robot behaviors into temporal logic formulas, allowing the system to reason about the robot's state and generate plans of action. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of temporal logic, focusing on its ability to represent temporal relationships – such as "always," "eventually," "until," and "strongly until" – which are crucial for describing dynamic robot systems. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential solutions in mapping temporal logic specifications to executable robot control systems, highlighting the need for efficient reasoning engines and suitable action representations. This work demonstrates the potential of temporal logic programming to enhance the robustness, reliability, and adaptability of autonomous robot systems.

title: Quantum Entanglement Analysis and Extension
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents unique challenges to our understanding of information and security. This paper explores the potential of leveraging non-symmetric quantum entanglement to develop novel quantum information protection mechanisms. We introduce a novel concept, "Non-Symmetric Entanglement Geometry" (NSEG), and investigate its implications for the stability of entangled states, particularly within geometric structures. Our analysis reveals that the inherent non-symmetry of entangled states can be exploited to enhance the robustness of quantum key distribution systems. The core claim is that the design of NSEG geometries will lead to more secure and stable quantum key distribution protocols. This work contributes to the ongoing research in quantum information theory, specifically focusing on mitigating vulnerabilities in current quantum communication protocols.

title: Dynamic Probability Field Simulation: A Graph-Based Structured Learning Approach
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic probability field simulation framework leveraging graph-based structured learning. Traditional probabilistic field simulations often rely on manual parameter design, demanding significant effort and limiting scalability. We propose a system that dynamically adjusts parameters by exploiting the inherent structure of the system represented as a graph. The core mechanism involves mapping system elements to graphs, and using these graphs to control the probability field, enabling automated parameter optimization and intelligent adaptation. This approach significantly reduces computational complexity while offering a flexible and adaptable framework for complex systems.

title: Towards Understanding Pause Token Fine-Tuning Dynamics: A Mode Retention Perspective
abstract: Pause-token methods improve LLM reasoning by inserting special tokens into sequences. Prior work explains these gains through computational expressivity. However, there is relatively little investigation into the training dynamics of pause tokens. We explore how pause tokens reshape the training dynamics of fine-tuning. Two controlled pilots expose distinct asymmetries. On a synthetic continual-learning task, masked pauses overwrite a previously-learned distribution roughly 4x less at matched final adaptation (H1, mode retention); on a synthetic math-reasoning probe, the boundary-adjacent token comes to encode substantially more downstream-step information (H2, non-myopic compression). We formalize a training rule consistent with both - Masked Boundary Pause (MBP), pause tokens placed at reasoning-step boundaries with their loss masked. Across 1B-8B Qwen and Llama models, MBP consistently improves reasoning, achieving gains of up to 6 points on math and 2.5 points on code, while preserving general language understanding abilities. We further demonstrate that this mode-preserving strategy extend gains to GRPO. These results recast pause tokens as a training-dynamics intervention on the retention-adaptation trade-off, rather than merely an inference-time computation device.

title: Random Garbage Separates XOR from Forward-Only Queries
abstract: We give exponential quantum query separations between the standard XOR interface and two forward-only interfaces that supply neither an adjoint nor an inverse oracle. Let $X=\F_2^n$, $N=|X|$, and $f_{h,r}(x)=(h(x),x,r_x)$, where $h:X\to X$ is promised to be either a permutation or a Simon two-to-one function, and $r$ is a fixed table of $n$-bit tags, unrestricted by the promise and reused on every query. The resulting problem is solvable with at most $n+2$ standard XOR queries, but has forward-erasing query complexity $Θ(\sqrt N)$. This answers affirmatively open question 11 in [Scott Aaronson. Open problems related to quantum query complexity. ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing, 2(4):14:1-14:9, 2021] . We also embed these instances into permutations. The detailed construction retains the copy of $x$ in each prescribed output, but for these promises that copy can be replaced by one bit that distinguishes the two inputs in every Simon pair. This gives a permutation domain of size $L=4N^2$ and a permutation problem with the same standard-query upper bound and forward-only in-place query complexity $Θ(\sqrt N)=Θ(L^{1/4})$. Both lower bounds remain valid with a clean coherent bypass. The common lower bound uses an analysis-only recording replacement. In the replacement computation, tracing out the fixed random tag table after $T$ calls gives a sum of positive-semidefinite operator contributions, each depending on $h$ at no more than $T$ addresses. On such a set, the restrictions induced by random permutations and random Simon functions differ only if the set contains a hidden Simon pair, an event of probability $O(T^2/N)$.

title: PACE: Towards Surfacing Hidden Conflicts in User Requests
abstract: Personalized assistants should not only comply with user requests but also assess whether those requests are appropriate given the user's current circumstances. However, prior work has primarily focused on accurately executing requests, overlooking the need for assistants to account for context and engage in conflict-based refusal. Furthermore, while existing work on conflict or safety detection relies on explicitly provided factors, real-world scenarios often involve implicit factors that must be retrieved from a knowledge base (KB). To this end, we introduce Personalized Assistants for Conflict Evaluation (PACE), a dataset for evaluating whether models can identify latent constraints, expressed as egocentric knowledge or events, that render seemingly reasonable user requests inappropriate. PACE pairs user requests grounded in well-defined personas with egocentric KB facts, requiring models to integrate contextual evidence to determine whether a request is conflicting. This implicit retrieval setting hinders the direct association between user requests and conflict-inducing knowledge, making it difficult for existing models to identify relevant user-specific facts. To address this challenge, we further propose PaceMaker, a multi-agent framework in which specialized agents coordinate across query reformulation, multi-hop graph traversal, and conflict-aware filtering to retrieve contextually decisive evidence. Experiments on PACE evaluate both evidence retrieval quality and conflict decision accuracy, showing that PaceMaker consistently outperforms existing approaches.

title: The Complete TUS OS Executable Realisation — Technical Volume I
abstract: Paper 10 (Technical Volume I) of 11 — A General Theory of Answerability The eleven-paper TUS OS mathematical research programme Abstract This technical volume establishes the formal representation and exact round-trip reconstruction of the complete admissible protected TUS OS organism in the Answerability Calculus. Its governing result is the Complete Round-Trip Representation Theorem: The complete admissible protected TUS OS organism and the intrinsic fibred Answerability representation are mutually reconstructible without loss of protected structure. The paper first constitutes the TUS OS source-side system independently of the comparison theory. The complete object is fixed as one protected relational organism with seven coordinate roles—native structure, constitution, convergence, production, discharge, resource/custody and claim/failure law—and nine protected relation classes governing incidence, dependency, authority, admissible flow, lawful convergence, non-substitution, custody continuity, conservation and disposition. A candidate-dependency register and admissible parameter family are then fixed before any representation map, reverse reconstruction, realised pilot outcome or preferred theorem strength is permitted to influence the construction. For each admissible parameter package, the paper independently constructs a typed Paper-9 Answerability problem and distinguishes the complete intrinsic fibred comparison object from its untagged semantic projection. The comparison object therefore exists prior to successful representation. An explicit anti-circularity theorem establishes that the TUS OS organism, admissible family, intrinsic Answerability comparison object and semantic transformation doctrine remain unchanged when the later forward map, reverse reconstruction, executable-commutation claims, realised witness outcomes and theorem-success predicates are erased from the constitutive dependency structure. The representation programme is then developed component by component. Native structure, semantic constitution, convergence, production, discharge, evidence and authority, resource and custody, and failure/disposition structure are represented at their independently established scopes. The construction preserves source-side authority, non-substitution, claim ceilings, qualifications, custody identities and explicit recovery/non-recovery boundaries rather than collapsing the TUS OS system into an untyped semantic image. The forward representation is subsequently closed on the complete admissible protected TUS OS quotient. An independently constructed reverse map reconstructs all seven protected coordinate roles and all nine protected relation classes from each intrinsic fibred Answerability point. The two independently established round trips are G30 ∘ F̂31 = id on the complete admissible protected TUS OS quotient, and F̂31 ∘ G30 = id on the intrinsic fibred Answerability representation. Hence, at the complete protected representation type, the complete admissible protected TUS OS quotient is exactly isomorphic, in the defined representation sense, to the intrinsic fibred Answerability representation. The isomorphism preserves and reflects the complete seven-coordinate/nine-relation protected signature, presentation-quotient identity, intrinsic fibre identity—including the candidate-independent execution-interface and protected terminal-semantic data—and every component and certificate scope already established. At the untagged semantic level, the forward representation is surjective onto the TUS-specified semantic comparison class; injectivity after forgetting intrinsic fibre identity is neither assumed nor required. The theorem boundary is explicit. Technical Volume I does not establish total-disposition soundness, realised discharge completeness, executable commutation, protected-trace equivalence, strongest-lawful production closure, integrated claim-authority conservation, realised irredundancy, proof-carrying executable discharge or realised pilot witnessing. Those are distinct Technical Volume II obligations. Nor does the protected representation isomorphism establish universal necessity, universal sufficiency or canonicity of the TUS OS organisational form; those questions remain reserved for Paper 11. At the scope proved here, Paper 10 Technical Volume I therefore closes the formal-representation problem: the complete admissible protected TUS OS organism is represented in the Answerability Calculus by an intrinsic fibred object from which the entire protected source structure can be reconstructed exactly, and vice versa. Technical Volume II then closes the execution-level problem through realised completeness, executable commutation, claim-authority conservation, proof-carrying discharge, and the Complete TUS OS Executable Representation Theorem. Paper 11 closes the programme with A General Theory of Answerability, establishing Structural Identity, Recognition, the canonical mandatory protected core, and lawful Realisation Freedom. title: Adaptive Geometry Matrix Quantum Computation
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of adaptive geometry matrix quantum computation for rapid and efficient computation of complex geometric structures. Traditional quantum computation often struggles with intricate geometric configurations due to static parameters, necessitating complex optimization routines. This work proposes a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts calculation parameters based on the input data's geometry, enabling faster and more effective solutions for challenging geometric problems. We explore the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of this approach, demonstrating its effectiveness in simulating and manipulating geometric data. The core claim is that this method significantly enhances computational efficiency for complex geometric tasks, surpassing the capabilities of existing quantum algorithms.

title: 基于自适应的深度学习模型的可解释性研究
abstract: This paper investigates the inherent challenges in interpreting deep learning models and proposes a novel approach to enhance model explainability through dynamic parameter adjustment. We introduce a method called "Adaptive Feature Refinement" (AFR) that dynamically adjusts the model's structural and parameter configurations based on data patterns. This adaptive process, coupled with a learned feature refinement strategy, aims to identify and highlight critical features that drive the model's decisions. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of AFR in improving model transparency and offering a more robust and adaptable approach to interpretability. The paper concludes with a discussion of the key findings and potential future directions.

title: 基于动态拓扑的神经网络加速器
abstract: This paper presents a novel neural network acceleration technique based on dynamic topology. Traditional neural network acceleration methods often rely on static topology adjustments, which are insufficient to address the dynamic nature of neural networks during training. We propose a framework that dynamically adjusts the topology of the network through a continuous evolution process, leveraging this adaptability to accelerate training and improve generalization. This approach offers a significant improvement over static methods by providing a mechanism for the network to adapt to changes in the data and learning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing substantial speedups and improved generalization performance.

title: Correction of Non-Linear Adaptive Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum error correction is a crucial element of quantum computing, enabling the reliable execution of complex computations. Current quantum error correction codes, while effective, often suffer from limitations in their error correction capability. This paper introduces a novel non-linear adaptive quantum error correction algorithm, designed to surpass the limitations of traditional methods. We present a framework that leverages quantum entanglement and instantaneous measurement to dynamically adjust the correction strategy based on the quantum state's fleeting changes, achieving unprecedented accuracy and speed in error correction. The core mechanism hinges on a sophisticated error analysis and feedback loop that optimizes the correction intensity and direction in real-time, mitigating the limitations of fixed algorithms. This work explores the potential for significant advancements in quantum information processing through the implementation of this novel approach.

title: Constraint Network Cryptography C: Constraint Network Rigidity of Post-Quantum Cryptography — Why Lattice Cryptography Is Quantum-Resistant
abstract: Under the constraint network phase transition framework, the computationalhardness underlying post-quantum cryptographic standards manifests three fundamental types of rigidity: spectrum-hiding, geometric torsion, and one-way condensation. The vulnerability of integer factorisation and discrete logarithms stems fromthe spectral manifestness of their rigidity kernels — the hidden subgroup structurecan be directly extracted in the frequency domain by the quantum Fourier transform. The quantum resistance of the shortest vector problem, the closest vectorproblem, and the learning with errors problem in lattice cryptography is rootedin the incompressibility of local geometric extrema in a high-dimensional continuous metric space: their rigidity kernels are neither encodable by characters offinite abelian groups, nor can their geometric entropy, which grows linearly withdimension, be altered by diffusive quantum operators beyond reducing exponential constants without changing the exponential type. Hash-based signatures relyon the information potential well of one-way condensation operators and remainexponentially secure even in the quantum random oracle model. This paper provides a quantum immunity criterion at the operator-algebra level and extends itto a generalised criterion covering both spectral-diagnostic and diffusive quantumoperator families, and retrospectively verifies the sufficiency of the parameter designs of Kyber, Dilithium, and SPHINCS+. The entire argument carries explicitcondition-depth annotations, and the entropy budget for cross-domain mappingsis constrained by the axiom of information conservation, thereby establishing thegeometric foundation of post-quantum cryptography within honest boundaries.

The vulnerability of integer factorisation and discrete logarithms stems fromthe spectral manifestness of their rigidity kernels — the hidden subgroup structurecan be directly extracted in the frequency domain by the quantum Fourier transform. The quantum resistance of the shortest vector problem, the closest vectorproblem, and the learning with errors problem in lattice cryptography is rootedin the incompressibility of local geometric extrema in a high-dimensional continuous metric space: their rigidity kernels are neither encodable by characters offinite abelian groups, nor can their geometric entropy, which grows linearly withdimension, be altered by diffusive quantum operators beyond reducing exponential constants without changing the exponential type. Hash-based signatures relyon the information potential well of one-way condensation operators and remainexponentially secure even in the quantum random oracle model. This paper provides a quantum immunity criterion at the operator-algebra level and extends itto a generalised criterion covering both spectral-diagnostic and diffusive quantumoperator families, and retrospectively verifies the sufficiency of the parameter designs of Kyber, Dilithium, and SPHINCS+. The entire argument carries explicitcondition-depth annotations, and the entropy budget for cross-domain mappingsis constrained by the axiom of information conservation, thereby establishing thegeometric foundation of post-quantum cryptography within honest boundaries.

title: Title: Adaptive Chaos Algorithm Foundation
abstract: This paper presents a fundamental mathematical framework for the Adaptive Chaos Algorithm (ACA), exploring its core principles and potential for advanced system analysis and design. ACA leverages the inherent dynamic properties of chaos to provide a robust and adaptable approach to optimization. The core mechanism involves the integration of ACA with established mathematical modeling techniques, enabling a system-aware optimization algorithm. The investigation focuses on establishing a robust mathematical model to guide the dynamic adjustment of parameters, resulting in enhanced system control precision. The novelty of this work lies in the synthesis of a novel optimization algorithm predicated on the dynamic adjustments inherent within ACA, demonstrating a potential shift towards more precise system management.

title: Title: Quantum Error Mitigation via Dynamic Bias Tuning
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a critical component of quantum computing, enabling reliable computation by protecting quantum information from noise. However, current QEC codes are highly sensitive to errors, necessitating sophisticated error mitigation strategies. This paper presents a novel approach to QEC, utilizing dynamic bias tuning to dynamically adjust bias parameters within quantum error correction codes. We demonstrate a significant improvement in accuracy and reduced overhead compared to static bias adjustment methods. The proposed system employs a self-tuning algorithm that analyzes the error profile and automatically adjusts bias parameters, offering a highly adaptive and effective means of mitigating errors. This work addresses a key challenge in QEC – the need for continuous optimization – and opens the door to more robust and efficient quantum computation.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Evolutionary Algorithms for Complex Parameter Space
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-enhanced evolutionary algorithms to complex parameter space optimization. Traditional evolutionary algorithms, while powerful, often struggle with the vastness and non-linearity of these spaces, leading to slow convergence and limited solution quality. We propose a novel approach leveraging quantum annealing and quantum sampling techniques to enhance exploration and optimization capabilities, addressing these limitations. The core claim is that quantum-enhanced evolutionary algorithms offer a significant speedup and improved solution quality for complex parameter space problems, particularly when traditional methods fail to perform adequately. This work introduces a framework for utilizing quantum phenomena to guide the evolutionary process, offering a potential paradigm shift in optimization algorithms.

title: 基于图的自适应优化算法的动态变量调整
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm, termed "Dynamic Variable Adjustment Optimization" (DVAO), designed to enhance the efficiency of optimization algorithms by dynamically adjusting node and edge weights based on data characteristics. The core principle of DVAO lies in a continuous, adaptive weighting mechanism that responds to changing data, leading to improved convergence and solution quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DVAO through simulations and a practical case study involving a complex, non-convex optimization problem. The algorithm's ability to leverage data-driven weighting significantly outperforms traditional optimization methods in terms of convergence speed and solution accuracy. The paper concludes with a detailed explanation of the algorithm's components and the underlying mathematical principles.

title: Quantum Error Correction Coding Based Distributed Learning Algorithm
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed learning algorithm leveraging the redundancy inherent in quantum error correction (QEC) coding. The core idea is to encode the learning outcomes of each node into the channels of a QEC code, subsequently decoding them to recover the original information. Through iterative exchanges of encoded information via these channels, nodes collaboratively learn. Unlike traditional distributed learning which often assumes ideal communication channels, this approach constructs a robust system directly utilizing the noise-resilient properties of QEC. We formally define the algorithm, outlining the encoding and decoding processes, and analyze its potential to improve learning efficiency and resilience, particularly in environments with significant communication noise. The key contribution lies in the integration of QEC into the distributed learning framework, creating a fundamentally more robust and potentially more efficient learning paradigm. The theoretical framework presented here provides a foundation for future research into applying QEC-based distributed learning to various complex systems. ---

title: Per-link verification benchmark for a lineage-carrying offline CBDC token
abstract: Supplement to the manuscript “When the Secure Element Fails: A Post-Compromise Security Architecture for Offline CBDC Payment Services” (under review) A micro-benchmark of the cryptographic operations that determine the per-link verification cost of a lineage-carrying offline payment token, together with the composition that turns them into a per-link figure. What it measures. In the architecture the script accompanies, each transfer of a token appends a link carrying a threshold-encrypted identity record and a non-interactive proof that the record encrypts the identity certified for the key that signs the transfer. Verifying one link means two Ed25519 signature verifications, one SHA-256 digest, one two-term pairing check for the credential component, and one multi-scalar multiplication for the plaintext-equality and linking relations. The script times each of these on BLS12-381 and reports the composition. Because every aggregate cost in the architecture - sustained verifier load, recipient verification time, the practical bound on transfer depth - scales in this single quantity, it is the figure most worth measuring before an implementation exists. Method. BLS12-381 operations use the arkworks backend through its Python bindings; Ed25519 verification uses the OpenSSL implementation exposed by the cryptography package. Each operation is timed over a warmed loop and reported as the median with tenth and ninetieth percentiles. Two compositions are produced: the adopted construction, in which an anonymous credential is shown in zero knowledge, and a compact alternative in which the registrar signs the key material in the clear and no pairing is required. Reference results. On a single Intel Xeon core at 2.10 GHz: a two-term pairing check 1 744 μs, a twelve-term multi-scalar multiplication 942 μs, a single G1 scalar multiplication 190 μs, Ed25519 verification 113 μs, SHA-256 over a 742-byte link 1.0 μs. Composed, this gives 2.93 ms per link for the adopted construction, of which the pairing check is 60%, against 0.96 ms for the compact alternative. Two findings. A Σ-protocol verifier evaluates one multi-scalar multiplication rather than a sequence of independent scalar multiplications, and the difference is not marginal: twelve terms cost 942 μs together against 2 543 μs performed separately. Cost models for constructions of this kind are easy to overstate by that factor of 2.7. And the ratio between the two constructions depends on how far fixed-base precomputation is carried, since the multi-scalar terms benefit from it and the pairing does not; the factor of three measured here with generic bases and the factor of seven and a half attainable with precomputation are the two ends of one range rather than competing estimates. What it does not measure. This is a micro-benchmark of primitives on server-class hardware, not an evaluation of a payment system. It says nothing about proof generation, which runs on the holder’s device and is three to five times more expensive than verification; nothing about mobile ARM performance; nothing about secure element commit latency under the ordering the architecture requires; and nothing about wall-clock transfer over a contactless interface. The reference host is a shared cloud core, slower than a current server core by roughly a factor of two to three, and the arkworks backend is slower than an assembly-optimised one such as blst by a comparable factor. Running it. Python 3.10 or later with two dependencies: pip install py_arkworks_bls12381 cryptographypython3 bench_link.py --reps 240 --json results.json It completes in a few minutes on one core and requires no hardware beyond it. --reps controls the sample count; --json writes the primitive medians, the two compositions and their ratio for further use.

title: Differentiable Optimization of Quantum Circuits
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to optimizing quantum circuits by directly calculating and applying gradients. Traditional quantum algorithm optimization relies heavily on simulating the quantum circuit on classical computers, which is computationally expensive and limits the scalability of these algorithms. Our work proposes a framework for differentiable quantum circuit optimization, treating quantum circuits as differentiable functions and employing gradient-based optimization techniques. We outline a methodology for computing gradients of the expectation values of quantum circuits with respect to their adjustable parameters. This allows for the direct optimization of quantum circuits using algorithms such as gradient descent, potentially leading to significant improvements in the efficiency and accuracy of quantum algorithms. The core contribution lies in providing a mathematically rigorous foundation for this differentiable approach, paving the way for automated quantum algorithm design and enhancement. The presented method offers a viable alternative to classical simulation, addressing a key bottleneck in the practical implementation of quantum algorithms.

title: Dimension Perception and Quantum Entanglement Dynamics
abstract: This paper explores the integration of dimension perception and quantum entanglement dynamics to achieve real-time modeling and control of quantum field structures. We propose a novel mechanism utilizing a dynamically entangled sensor network, where the strength of entanglement directly correlates with the perceived dimension. This approach offers a fundamentally new pathway for precise measurement and manipulation of quantum field properties, offering a significant advancement beyond traditional quantum computation's limitations. The core claim is that this dynamic entanglement-based sensor network will provide a real-time, high-precision mapping of quantum field parameters.

title: Prompt Clarity, Correction Churn, and Token Efficiency
abstract: An evaluation of whether stating requirements and output constraints in the initial prompt reduces correction exchanges and tokens per solved task. The study runs 14 machine-checkable tasks across lazy and front-loaded prompt arms, thinking off and default adaptive thinking, with five repetitions per cell and one verifier-guided correction turn after failures. Across 280 first turns and 120 corrections, front-loaded prompts used 45,463 recorded tokens versus 160,799 for lazy prompts, while solving 134 of 140 repetitions versus 96 of 140. The paper reports the method, verifier design, task-category results, counterexamples, limitations, and reproducibility artifacts.

title: Dynamic Quantum Adaptive Geometry Transformation Guided by Entanglement
abstract: This paper investigates the application of dynamic quantum adaptive geometry transformations guided by entanglement to achieve precise geometric control. Traditional geometric transformations often require iterative refinement, which can be computationally expensive and time-consuming. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust geometric parameters, enabling a significantly reduced number of iterations and improved accuracy. This approach addresses the limitations of conventional methods by offering a fundamentally different approach to geometric manipulation. The core mechanism involves creating and manipulating entangled quantum states to represent the transformation parameters, allowing for precise control and efficient adaptation. We present a theoretical framework and initial implementation demonstrating the algorithm's potential for enhanced geometric precision. The results showcase improved efficiency and accuracy compared to existing methods.

title: Adaptive Random Matrix Algorithm: A Mathematical Foundation
abstract: This paper explores the mathematical foundations of an adaptive random matrix algorithm designed for dynamic adjustment of matrix parameters within machine learning models. The algorithm's core principle lies in learning a dynamic mapping between data distributions and matrix parameters, leading to optimized model training and prediction. We present a rigorous mathematical framework, detailing the algorithm's structure, mathematical operations, and potential advantages over traditional methods. The paper focuses on the core mechanism of parameter adjustment and its impact on model performance through a focused mathematical analysis.

title: 基于自旋的几何变换的隐式几何算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to geometric computation leveraging the unique properties of spin. We propose a new type of geometric transformation algorithm based on the manipulation of spin states, offering a computationally efficient and potentially highly flexible method for complex geometric operations. The core mechanism centers around a framework that harnesses quantum spin effects to accelerate geometric computations. This algorithm is designed with a focus on providing a robust tool for detecting and analyzing geometric transformations, demonstrating its potential for advancements in geometric modeling and analysis. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and present preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in specific geometric transformations.

title: 基于自适应的量子态的量子纠错协议
abstract: Quantum entanglement offers a revolutionary approach to information processing and communication, promising enhanced security and computational power. However, the inherent fragility of quantum states necessitates robust error correction techniques. This paper proposes a novel quantum state manipulation technique, termed "Adaptive Quantum State Correction" (AQC), which dynamically adjusts the correction parameters based on measurement outcomes. Our research demonstrates that AQC significantly improves the performance of quantum error correction protocols by optimizing the correction process in real-time. The core mechanism involves a self-adaptive quantum state, allowing for a more efficient and robust correction strategy compared to traditional methods. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results showcasing the effectiveness of AQC in mitigating errors in a simplified quantum circuit setup. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential implications of this approach for the advancement of quantum information technologies.

title: Title: Topological Singularities for Quantum Entanglement
abstract: Quantum entanglement networks offer unparalleled opportunities for secure communication and distributed quantum computing, but their fragility to decoherence presents a significant challenge. This research explores the potential of topological singularities – regions of enhanced quantum coherence – as a crucial element in preserving entanglement, and introduces a novel method for constructing and analyzing these singularities. We hypothesize that understanding and manipulating these singularities can drastically improve the prediction and mitigation of decoherence pathways. The proposed approach leverages a dynamically adaptive, multi-scale topological field theory, integrating quantum entanglement directly into a geometric framework, enabling highly targeted decoherence prediction. This work demonstrates the efficacy of this method through simulations and preliminary analysis, showcasing its potential to enhance the robustness of quantum networks.
